# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Effective jurisdiction:** Spanish Louisiana — Arkansas was not a separate jurisdiction before 1800; it existed as the remote upper district of the Spanish Province of Louisiana, administered from New Orleans
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (*Puesto de los Arkansás*), the only sustained European settlement, located at the confluence of the Arkansas and Mississippi rivers
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Louisiana (Spanish), with superior authority ultimately in Havana (Captaincy General of Cuba) and Madrid
- **Population during period:** Extremely small — Arkansas Post had only a few hundred European settlers and soldiers at any given time during the Spanish period; the broader territory's European population was negligible outside the Post
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, garrison provisioning
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers (the majority of the civilian population retained French culture and language throughout Spanish rule), Spanish military officers and administrators, enslaved Africans, and the Quapaw Nation (the dominant indigenous group in the region)
- **Religious denomination:** Roman Catholic (exclusively); the Church was the primary institutional record-keeper
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris (1763) transferred French Louisiana to Spain; Spain administered the region until secretly ceding it back to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso (1800); the Louisiana Purchase (1803) then transferred everything to the United States

---

## Boundary Changes and Jurisdictional Succession

This is a two-phase temporal split — a clean before/after rule applies at each transition:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Administrative Authority |
|---|---|---|
| 1686–1763 | French Louisiana (*La Louisiane*) | Paris / Superior Council, New Orleans |
| 1763–1800 | Spanish Louisiana | Madrid / Havana / Governor-General, New Orleans |
| 1800–1803 | French Louisiana (brief retrocession) | Paris |
| 1803–1819 | United States — Territory of Orleans / District of Louisiana | Washington, D.C. |
| 1819–1836 | Arkansas Territory | U.S. federal government |
| 1836– | State of Arkansas | State government, Little Rock |

**Research rule:** Records created before 1800 were created under French or Spanish colonial authority, not Arkansas authority. Search under Louisiana colonial record systems — not Arkansas state or county systems — for this period. Records held in Little Rock are copies or transcriptions; originals often remain in European archives.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records (Sacramental Registers) — PRIMARY SOURCE FOR THIS PERIOD

**This is the most important record category for pre-1800 Arkansas.** Catholic missionaries maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post covering baptisms, marriages, and burials of European settlers, soldiers, enslaved persons, and some Native Americans.

- **Date range (French period):** Early 1700s through 1763 — surviving registers held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and in transcribed form at the Arkansas History Commission ([Arkansas Genealogy, Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Date range (Spanish period):** 1763–1800 — one digitized FamilySearch volume survives: **Image Group 008814402**, 64 images, covering Arkansas Post 1763–1800
  - ⚠️ **Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed page by page
  - ⚠️ **Language: Spanish** — records require ability to read colonial-era Spanish (and sometimes French or Latin)
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch (browse-only): Image Group [008814402](https://www.familysearch.org/search/)
  - Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives — original registers
  - Arkansas History Commission — transcribed copies
- **Language warning:** Even under Spanish administration, most civilian settlers were French Creoles; registers may alternate between Spanish and French entries

**Louisiana overlap:** FamilySearch collection **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (Collection ID [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905), ~987,654 records) covers the same Catholic diocese system that administered Arkansas Post. Records from the Arkansas district were sometimes registered through New Orleans. Search this Louisiana collection in parallel with the Arkansas Post volumes.

---

### Census Records (Padrones / Population Enumerations)

The Spanish colonial government conducted household censuses called **padrones** — enumerated lists of heads of household, family members, servants, and enslaved persons at each settlement.

- **Date range:** Several padrones of Arkansas Post survive from the Spanish period (1763–1800), documenting the small settler population
- **Indexed FamilySearch collection:** "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870" (Collection ID [2085124](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2085124), ~178,345 records) — starts in 1819, **after** the Spanish period, but may incorporate earlier substitute enumerations; verify coverage before assuming it excludes colonial-era padrones
- **Where surviving padrones are held:**
  - Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock — transcriptions and some originals
  - Library of Congress — microfilm copies of Spanish colonial records from Louisiana
  - Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville, Spain — original Spanish administrative records including padrones for Louisiana Province ([Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Access level:** Physical only (AHC, AGI) or microfilm (Library of Congress) — no name-indexed online database covers pre-1800 Arkansas padrones as a distinct collection

---

### Land Records (Concesiones de Tierras / Land Concessions)

Spanish authorities issued land concessions (*concesiones*) to settlers at Arkansas Post. These are among the most genealogically valuable records of the period because they name grantees, sometimes neighbors and witnesses, and describe property locations.

- **Critical survival path:** After the Louisiana Purchase, the U.S. government was obligated by treaty to honor valid Spanish land grants. The Board of Land Commissioners reviewed thousands of claims in the early 1800s, producing English-language transcriptions and translations of the underlying Spanish concessions. These English transcriptions survive even when originals are lost
- **Where held:**
  - Arkansas History Commission — Spanish land grant files and U.S. Board of Land Commissioners records
  - BLM General Land Office (GLO) Records ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) — some Spanish-era patents confirmed under U.S. authority appear here
  - National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA Southwest Region) — territorial-era land claim files
  - AGI, Seville — original Spanish concession records for Louisiana Province
- **Access level:** Physical only or microfilm for the colonial originals; some U.S.-period transcriptions are available online via BLM GLO

---

### Military Records

Arkansas Post was a military garrison throughout the Spanish period. Military records document soldiers and officers stationed there.

- **Record types:** Muster rolls, garrison lists, service records, officer correspondence
- **Where held:**
  - AGI, Seville — primary repository for Spanish colonial military records of Louisiana Province
  - Archivo General Militar de Simancas (Simancas, Spain) — Spanish military service records
  - Library of Congress — some microfilmed copies
  - Arkansas History Commission — some transcriptions
- **Access level:** Physical only (Spain) or microfilm (Library of Congress); nothing is online in a name-indexed format for this specific location and period
- **Note on Fold3:** Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) holds some U.S. military records but has minimal coverage of Spanish colonial garrison records; do not rely on it for this period

---

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **None exist for this period.** There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in colonial Arkansas. The Catholic Church's sacramental registers (above) are the functional equivalent and the only systematic record of vital events
- Civil registration in Arkansas did not begin until the late nineteenth century, long after statehood (1836)

---

### Probate and Court Records

- **Very limited.** A small civil court operated at Arkansas Post under Spanish authority, handling disputes, successions, and contracts
- **Louisiana parallel:** The Superior Council of Louisiana (New Orleans) had appellate jurisdiction; some Arkansas Post matters appear in Louisiana provincial court records
- **Where held:**
  - Arkansas History Commission — some transcriptions of post-level court records
  - Louisiana State Archives / Historic New Orleans Collection — Louisiana Superior Council records that may include Arkansas Post cases
  - FamilySearch collection **"Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984"** (Collection ID [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341), ~456,789 records, date range overlaps the Spanish period from 1756) — search this for any estates or successions that passed through New Orleans
- **Access level:** Indexed + images for the Louisiana probate FamilySearch collection; physical only for most original post-level records

---

### Tax Records

- Spanish colonial administrators levied taxes and tribute; records documenting taxpayers and property valuations survive intermittently
- **Where held:** AGI, Seville; some at Library of Congress on microfilm; Arkansas History Commission holds transcriptions
- **Substitute value:** When padrones are missing, tax/tribute records can place a person at a location in a specific year

---

### Cemetery and Burial Records

- Burials at Arkansas Post were recorded primarily in the Catholic sacramental registers (see Church Records above) rather than in separate sexton registers
- Physical grave markers from the colonial period have largely not survived
- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) has negligible coverage of pre-1800 Arkansas burials; do not rely on it for this period

---

### Immigration / Migration Records

- No formal immigration records exist for this period in the modern sense; Arkansas Post residents arrived through New Orleans or overland from other French/Spanish colonies
- **Passenger lists for New Orleans** (arriving from France, Spain, or the Caribbean) may document the origins of settlers who later appeared at Arkansas Post — check NARA records and the Historic New Orleans Collection

---

### Newspaper Records

- No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800; New Orleans had a French-language *Gazette de la Louisiane* but it did not cover Arkansas Post in any systematic way
- No relevant newspaper archive applies to this period and place

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Relevant Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers 1763–1800 (Image Group 008814402, browse-only, 64 images, Spanish); Louisiana Church Records 1718–1925 (Collection 1612905, indexed); Louisiana Probate Records 1756–1984 (Collection 2078341, indexed); Arkansas Census Substitutes 1819–1870 (Collection 2085124, indexed — post-1800 only) | Free |
| **BLM GLO Records** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Spanish land grant patents confirmed under U.S. authority | Free |
| **Ancestry** | U.S. federal census collection (starts 1790 — Arkansas appears sparsely; not relevant to the Spanish period itself) | Subscription |
| **NARA Online** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)) | Some Louisiana Purchase-era land claim files accessible through NARA's online catalog | Free to search; copies may require fees |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access Method |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) | Spanish colonial records for Arkansas Post: padrones, land concessions, court records, transcribed sacramental registers; primary in-state repository | In-person or written inquiry; some finding aids online |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock Archives** (Little Rock, AR) | Original sacramental registers from Arkansas Post (baptisms, marriages, burials); French missionary-period records | Contact diocese archives directly |
| **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)** (Seville, Spain) | Original Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana Province, including Arkansas Post — padrones, land concessions, military records, correspondence | In-person (Seville) or request digital reproductions via [pares.mcu.es](https://pares.mcu.es); the *Papeles de Cuba* and *Papeles de Santo Domingo* series are the most relevant for Louisiana/Arkansas |
| **Archivo General Militar de Simancas** (Simancas, Spain) | Spanish military service records for officers and soldiers stationed at Arkansas Post | In-person or written inquiry |
| **Library of Congress** (Washington, D.C.) | Microfilm copies of Spanish colonial Louisiana records, including Arkansas-area materials | In-person (Microform Reading Room); some digitized through LC's online catalog |
| **Historic New Orleans Collection / Louisiana State Museum** (New Orleans, LA) | Louisiana Superior Council records, New Orleans colonial-era records that include Arkansas Post matters | In-person; some finding aids and digitized items at [hnoc.org](https://www.hnoc.org) |
| **NARA Southwest Region — Fort Worth** (Fort Worth, TX) | Early U.S. territorial-era land claim files reviewing Spanish grants | In-person or NARA online catalog |

---

## Records NOT Online (for the Pre-1800 Period)

The following record types are known to exist but have **no online name-indexed database** covering them for Arkansas before 1800:

- Spanish colonial padrones (household censuses) at Arkansas Post
- Spanish land concession originals (some U.S.-era transcriptions are online via BLM GLO)
- Military garrison records (muster rolls, officer rosters) at Arkansas Post
- Post-level civil court records
- Tax and tribute records
- French-period missionary registers predating 1763

The one digitized FamilySearch volume (Image Group 008814402) is browse-only and in Spanish — it is the sole online digital resource specifically targeting pre-1800 Arkansas.

---

## Known Record Losses and Gaps

- **Arkansas Post was attacked and damaged multiple times** — including by Chickasaw raids in the French period and the American assault on the Post during the Civil War (1863). These events destroyed some physical records at the site itself
- **Retention in European archives:** Many original Spanish colonial records were never held in Arkansas — they traveled with the colonial bureaucracy and now reside in Seville or Madrid. Their survival rate is generally better in the AGI than at the local level
- **French-period records (1686–1763):** More fragmentary than the Spanish-period records; surviving registers are held by the Diocese of Little Rock and AHC, but gaps are significant
- **Population was tiny:** Even comprehensive survival of all colonial records would document only a few hundred individuals across the entire Spanish period

---

## Research Tips

1. **Arkansas Post is the only place to research.** Virtually all pre-1800 European settler activity in what is now Arkansas was concentrated at or near Arkansas Post. If your ancestor was in the region, they were almost certainly connected to this settlement ([Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

2. **Search under Louisiana, not Arkansas.** All colonial-era record systems were administered through New Orleans. Search FamilySearch's Louisiana collections alongside the one Arkansas Post volume; check the Louisiana church records (Collection 1612905) and Louisiana probate records (Collection 2078341) for individuals who moved between Arkansas Post and New Orleans

3. **The AGI in Seville is indispensable.** For any serious research into Spanish colonial Arkansas, the Archivo General de Indias is the authoritative repository. Specifically, search the *Papeles de Cuba* series (which covers the Captaincy General of Cuba, the administrative umbrella for Louisiana) at [pares.mcu.es](https://pares.mcu.es). Many documents have been digitized and are accessible online through the PARES portal without travel

4. **Spanish land grants have an American paper trail.** The U.S. Board of Land Commissioners (1805–1812) reviewed all prior Spanish grants in the Louisiana Purchase territory. Their proceedings generated English-language abstracts and translations of Spanish documents, held at NARA Fort Worth and the Arkansas History Commission — these are often easier to access than the original Spanish documents

5. **Language of records:** Despite Spanish political control (1763–1800), most civilian settlers were French Creoles. Records from Arkansas Post mix French and Spanish — sometimes within the same register. Researchers need reading ability in both colonial Spanish and 18th-century French, plus some Latin for Catholic sacramental formulae

6. **The FamilySearch browse-only volume requires patience.** Image Group 008814402 (64 images of Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800) has zero name indexing. Browse it sequentially at FamilySearch. Given the small population, a complete browse is feasible ([Arkansas Genealogy, Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))

7. **Check transcription and publication projects.** The Arkansas Historical Quarterly and various genealogical society publications have printed transcriptions of colonial Arkansas records. The Arkansas Genealogical Society and the Arkansas History Commission have published finding aids that are worth consulting before traveling to Seville

8. **Native American context:** The Quapaw were the dominant people in the region and appear in Catholic baptismal and marriage records at Arkansas Post — sometimes recorded by French or Spanish names given at baptism. If your research touches on Quapaw ancestry, sacramental registers and later federal records (post-1803) are the key sources

---

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Pre-Statehood, Circa 1790)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Governing authority in 1790:** Northwest Territory (established by the Northwest Ordinance, July 13, 1787). Ohio did not exist as a jurisdiction — the standardPlace `Ohio, United States` begins only in 1803.
- **First county organized within the territory:** Washington County (1788), centered on Marietta, covering virtually all of what would become Ohio. Hamilton County (encompassing the Cincinnati area) followed in 1790.
- **Statehood:** March 1, 1803 — the first state carved from the Northwest Territory.
- **Territorial capital:** Marietta (seat of the Northwest Territory's court and government during the target period).
- **Population:** No population data was returned by the tools for this period. Euro-American settlement of the Ohio country was in its very earliest stages ca. 1790; the area had been largely inaccessible due to ongoing conflicts with Native nations until the Treaty of Greenville (1795).
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trading, early land speculation. The Ohio Company of Associates (Marietta), Symmes Purchase (Cincinnati), Virginia Military District, and Connecticut Western Reserve each drove distinct settlement patterns.
- **Ethnic/religious composition:** Early settlers were primarily English, Scots-Irish, and German, with Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, and Quaker congregations among the earliest organized. German Reformed and Lutheran settlers concentrated in areas adjacent to Pennsylvania.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); founding of Marietta (1788, first permanent Euro-American settlement); ongoing conflict with Native nations (Northwest Indian War) through 1794; Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Treaty of Greenville (1795) opened most of Ohio to settlement; statehood (1803).

---

## Boundary Changes

This is one of the most consequential complexities for 1790 Ohio research:

**1. The Northwest Territory → Ohio (temporal split, 1787–1803)**
Ohio as a jurisdiction did not exist in 1790. All civil authority — courts, land grants, early marriages — rested with the territorial government of the Northwest Territory and with the two counties it had organized by then (Washington, 1788; Hamilton, 1790). Records created before March 1, 1803 are therefore *territorial records*, not Ohio state records. The before/after rule is clean: before March 1803, look to Washington County or Hamilton County records and to the territorial courts at Marietta; after March 1803, look to Ohio county-level records and the Ohio State Archives.

**2. Washington County as the original parent (geographic cascade)**
Washington County (1788) initially covered all of the future state. As settlement grew, new counties were carved from it — but in 1790, only Washington and Hamilton existed. Which county held authority over an event in 1790 depended entirely on where within the territory the event occurred:
- **Southeastern Ohio / Marietta area** → Washington County (formed 1788)
- **Southwestern Ohio / Cincinnati area** → Hamilton County (formed 1790)
- **All other areas** → Still nominally Washington County, but in practice, civil infrastructure barely existed outside those two centers in 1790

Because the geographic split was ongoing and rapid after 1795, you must determine *which county* held jurisdiction at the *exact date* of the event. Early court and land records from this cascade of county formations are held at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus ([Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)).

**3. Distinct land-grant districts (geographic splits with separate record trails)**
Three districts within the future Ohio had entirely different land systems, each with records held in different repositories:

| District | Location | Survey System | Records Held At |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers (south-central Ohio) | Metes and bounds (not rectangular) | Virginia State Library (warrants); Ohio History Connection (entries) |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Connecticut grid survey | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **Seven Ranges / General Land Office** | Southeastern Ohio | First U.S. rectangular survey (1785) | BLM General Land Office (gloriouslandrecords.blm.gov) |
| **Ohio Company Purchase** | Around Marietta | Rectangular survey | Ohio History Connection |
| **Symmes Purchase** | Around Cincinnati | Rectangular survey | Ohio History Connection / NARA |

Which district your ancestor was in determines which repository holds their land records. These districts do *not* follow each other chronologically — they are geographically separate, and which applies depends entirely on where within the territory your ancestor settled. Search all that are plausible until the location is pinned down.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** Ohio did **not** have statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1790 — or for decades after. Statewide vital registration came much later and is entirely outside the 1790 window.
- **Marriage records (partial):** Individual counties began keeping marriage bonds and registers when organized. Washington County marriages begin **1789** and are captured in **FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013"** (collection ID 1803785; 1,523,678 records / 761,839 images; [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785)). This is the primary online source for marriages touching the 1790 period. **Indexed + images.**
- **Births and deaths:** No civil registration exists for the 1790 period. Church records and family bibles are the only contemporaneous documentation.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers, family bible records, cemetery headstones.

### Church Records
- **Denominations present ca. 1790:** Presbyterian (earliest organized congregations in Marietta and Washington County), Methodist (circuit riders active from late 1780s), Baptist, Quaker (Friends settled in the Muskingum Valley), German Reformed and Lutheran (in communities near the Pennsylvania border).
- **What exists:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; some membership rolls and minutes.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950"** (collection ID 2246917; 678,234 records / 339,117 images; [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917)) — this overlaps directly with the 1790 period. Accessibility level not confirmed from volume data; treat as **indexed** based on record count.
- **Physical repositories:** Denominational archives (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia; United Methodist Archives, Madison, NJ; Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore, PA); local congregation records at Ohio History Connection.
- **Language:** Records are in English for most denominations; German Reformed and Lutheran registers may be in German.
- **Critical note:** Church records are the *primary substitute* for the complete absence of civil vital registration in 1790. They should be the first stop for births and deaths in this period.

### Census Records
- **1790 federal census:** **The Northwest Territory was NOT included.** The First Census of 1790 covered only the original states. No federal enumeration exists for the Ohio country in 1790.
- **1800 federal census:** The first federal census to cover the area that became Ohio — taken while it was still the Northwest Territory. This is the earliest federal census available for Ohio-area families. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry; **indexed + images**.
- **Territorial enumeration:** No formal territorial census for 1790 has been identified in the tool results. Tax lists (see below) are the functional substitute.
- **State censuses:** Ohio conducted no statewide census for 1790. Some county-level militia and voter lists survive but are scattered.

### Tax Records
- **Territorial period:** **Volume search returned a Washington County, Ohio Tax Records volume covering 1799–1803** (imageGroupNumber 005112240; 73 images; 12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). This volume covers the very end of the territorial period and must be **browsed image-by-image for 88% of its content**; only 12% is reachable by name search.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850"** (collection ID 1987542; 345,890 records / 172,945 images; [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542)) — begins 1800, just outside the 1790 window, but captures families present from the territorial period onward.
- **Substitute value:** Because no census covers 1790 Ohio, tax lists are the closest functional equivalent for enumerating who was present. A family appearing in the 1800–1803 tax records almost certainly arrived during or before the 1790s.
- **Repository for pre-1800 territorial tax records:** Ohio History Connection, Columbus (physical or microfilm only; not confirmed as digitized by tool results).

### Land Records *(Most Important Record Type for 1790)*
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840"** (collection ID 1542187; 234,567 records / 117,283 images; [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187)) — begins 1787, directly covering the 1790 period. **Indexed + images.**
- **Territorial land records volume:** Volume search returned **Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799** (imageGroupNumber 005112233; 51 images; **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**). This volume must be **browsed image-by-image** — there is no name index. It covers the earliest documented land transactions in the Ohio country.
- **BLM General Land Office:** Federal land patents for Ohio are digitized at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — free, searchable. Covers original patents in the Seven Ranges, Ohio Company Purchase, Symmes Purchase, and other federal tracts.
- **Virginia Military District:** Warrants and surveys at the **Virginia State Library** (Richmond, VA); some entries also at Ohio History Connection ([Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)).
- **Connecticut Western Reserve:** Records at the **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland ([Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)).
- **System note:** Ohio is a **federal-land state** (not a state-land state). Original land titles derive from federal patents, not from state grants — this determines which repositories are authoritative.
- **Critical strategy:** For a 1790 ancestor, a land patent or entry is often the *only* surviving documentary evidence of their presence. Search land records before any other record type.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Washington County Probate:** Washington County's court of common pleas opened 1788. Some probate records from this period survive at the Washington County Courthouse and Ohio History Connection.
- **Territorial courts:** The Northwest Territory operated a general court at Marietta. Records from that court are held at the **Ohio History Connection**, Columbus — physical/microfilm, limited digitization confirmed by tool results.
- **Access:** Not confirmed as digitized from volume or collections search results. Treat as **physical or microfilm** for the 1790 period; contact Ohio History Connection directly.

### Military Records
- **Revolutionary War:** Many of the first Ohio settlers were Revolutionary War veterans who received Virginia Military District land warrants as bounty. Pension and bounty-land files are at **NARA** and accessible via [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription) — returned as a curated external link. These pension files often contain detailed biographical information including family relationships, dates, and migration history.
- **Northwest Indian War (1785–1795):** Militia service records for campaigns in the Ohio country (St. Clair's Defeat 1791, Battle of Fallen Timbers 1794) are at NARA and state adjutant general records. The Ohio History Connection holds Ohio militia records.
- **Access:** NARA records accessible via [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription) and some free via [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.

### Cemetery Records
- **Earliest cemeteries:** Pioneer burial grounds, church cemeteries, and private family plots from the late 1780s onward. Many pre-1800 graves are unmarked or headstones have not survived.
- **Online coverage:** [FindAGrave](https://www.findagrave.com/) (returned as a curated external link) covers many Ohio cemeteries; coverage for pre-1800 burials is sparse given the settlement period.
- **Physical:** Sexton records rarely survive for the 1790 period. DAR transcription projects and local historical society surveys are the best finding aids.

### Newspaper Records
- **Coverage in 1790:** Essentially none. The first Ohio newspaper, the *Centinel of the North-Western Territory*, began publication in Cincinnati in **November 1793** — after the target date. No newspapers existed in the Ohio country in 1790.
- **Post-1793:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (returned as a curated external link) holds some early Ohio papers; coverage before 1800 is very thin.
- **Note:** Newspapers are not a viable source for the 1790 period specifically.

### Immigration / Emigration Records
- **Context:** Most Ohio settlers in 1790 came overland from Pennsylvania, Virginia, and New England — not via transatlantic ports during this period. Passenger lists are not the primary record type here.
- **Migration trail:** Researchers should search records of the *origin* states (Pennsylvania, Virginia, Connecticut, New York, New England) alongside Ohio territorial records to reconstruct family history before and during the migration.
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable for most 1790 Ohio settlers, who were native-born American citizens. For immigrant settlers, pre-1906 naturalization could occur in any court of record; the territorial courts at Marietta handled some.

### DNA and Genetic Genealogy
- Given the near-total absence of vital registration for 1790, DNA evidence (autosomal, Y-DNA, mtDNA) is an especially important complement to documentary research. Connecting to established Colonial-era or Virginia pedigrees through DNA can bridge gaps in the Ohio territorial record.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for This Place & Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Ohio, County Marriages 1789–2013 (ID 1803785); Ohio, Church Records 1787–1950 (ID 2246917); Ohio, Land Records 1787–1840 (ID 1542187); Ohio, Tax Records 1800–1850 (ID 1987542); NW Territory Land Records 1788–1799 (browse-only vol. 005112233); Washington Co. Tax Records 1799–1803 (partially indexed vol. 005112240) | Free |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Original federal land patents for Ohio | Free — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **Ancestry** | U.S. Federal Census (1800 onward for Ohio); military records | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Revolutionary War pensions; Northwest Indian War militia | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery transcriptions statewide | Free |
| **NARA (online via Fold3/Ancestry)** | Pension files; bounty land warrants | Varies |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus, OH) | Territorial court records; early county records; county formation files; land entry records; militia records | In-person / some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| **NARA (Washington, D.C. / St. Louis)** | Revolutionary War service and pension records; federal land patents; 1800 census originals | In-person / mail / Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Washington County Courthouse** (Marietta, OH) | Washington County probate, deed, and marriage records from 1788 | In-person / mail |
| **Virginia State Library** (Richmond, VA) | Virginia Military District land warrants | In-person / correspondence |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society** (Cleveland, OH) | Connecticut Western Reserve land and settlement records | In-person |
| **Ohio Genealogical Society** (Bellville, OH) | Statewide indexes; county research files | In-person / mail |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following record types exist (or may exist) for 1790 Ohio but are **not confirmed as digitized** by the tool results:

- **Pre-1800 territorial court records** (Northwest Territory general court at Marietta) — physical at Ohio History Connection
- **Washington County probate records 1788–1799** — likely physical/microfilm at Ohio History Connection and Washington County Courthouse
- **Pre-1800 church registers** not captured in the FamilySearch church records collection — many local congregations have unpublished registers
- **Militia muster rolls, Northwest Indian War** — partly physical at Ohio History Connection and NARA
- **Family bible records** — widely scattered in family possession or local historical societies; not centrally indexed

---

## Known Record Losses and Gaps

- **No civil vital registration whatsoever** for the 1790 period. Births and deaths before county-level record-keeping began (1788 for Washington County) are essentially undocumented in civil records.
- **The 1790 federal census does not cover the Northwest Territory** — a complete gap. The 1800 census is the earliest federal enumeration.
- **Sparse settlement infrastructure:** In 1790, the Ohio country had only two organized counties (Washington and Hamilton), a handful of settlements, and active military conflict across much of the territory. Civil record-keeping was minimal and irregular. Many events simply went unrecorded.
- **Northwest Indian War disruption (1790–1795):** Active warfare across much of Ohio prevented settlement and record creation in large areas until after the Treaty of Greenville (1795). Do not expect meaningful records from areas outside the Marietta and Cincinnati corridors before 1795.
- **The Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records volume (005112233)** is entirely browse-only (0% indexed) — a significant access gap for the primary record type of the period.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with land, not vital records.** For 1790 Ohio, land patents and entries are the primary documentary anchor. A family's presence is most likely established first through a federal land patent (BLM GLO) or a Virginia Military District warrant. Build from land back to family ([Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)).

2. **Determine the land district first.** Before searching any Ohio land record, identify which district applies to your ancestor's location — Virginia Military District (metes and bounds, south-central Ohio), Connecticut Western Reserve (northeastern Ohio), or the federal rectangular surveys (southeastern/central Ohio). Each has its records in a different repository, and mixing them wastes time ([Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)).

3. **Know the county that existed at the event date.** In 1790, only Washington County and Hamilton County existed. Searching later county records (Adams, Clermont, Ross, etc.) for a 1790 event will fail — those counties did not exist. Work forward: start with Washington or Hamilton, then follow the county splits as your ancestor's community grew ([Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)).

4. **Search the origin state.** Many 1790 Ohio families are better documented in Pennsylvania, Virginia, New England, or New York than in Ohio itself. Reconstruct the family in the origin state before crossing into Ohio.

5. **Revolutionary War pensions are a gold mine.** Many early Ohio settlers were veterans. Pension application files at NARA (searchable on Fold3) frequently contain birth dates, marriage dates, children's names, migration history, and sworn depositions — far richer than anything in Ohio's sparse 1790 records.

6. **Browse the unindexed territorial land volume.** The Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records 1788–1799 (vol. 005112233 on FamilySearch) are 0% name-indexed and must be browsed image-by-image. This is painstaking but may be the only surviving documentation of a land transaction before Ohio statehood.

7. **The 1800 federal census is the earliest census anchor.** Use it to establish where a family was living at the start of the 19th century, then work backward through tax records and land entries to estimate their arrival in the Ohio country.

8. **Church records substitute for civil vital registration.** The FamilySearch "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" collection (ID 2246917) begins 1787 and is the primary substitute for absent civil birth and death records. Identify the denomination and search both the FamilySearch collection and the relevant denominational archives.

9. **Adjoining states share the record trail.** Families near the Ohio River generated records on both the Ohio and the Virginia/Kentucky side; families in northeastern Ohio may have records in western Pennsylvania. Search both sides of every border your ancestor lived near.

---

*Guide covers Ohio, United States (pre-statehood period, circa 1790). Standardized place: `Ohio, United States` (FamilySearch, from 1803); parent jurisdiction for 1790: Northwest Territory. Sources: FamilySearch collections search, volume search, external links search; FamilySearch Wiki search ([Ohio Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)); Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio). Wiki place pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned generic content only for this jurisdiction.*

---

The core takeaway for your 1790 Ohio research: **the jurisdiction didn't exist yet**, civil vital registration was zero, and the 1790 federal census skipped the territory entirely. Your three most productive starting points are **(1) federal land patents** at the BLM GLO, **(2) Revolutionary War pension files** at NARA/Fold3, and **(3) Washington or Hamilton County records** (marriage bonds from 1789, and the browse-only territorial land volume on FamilySearch). Church records fill the gap left by absent vital registration. Everything else in this period requires either physical visits to the Ohio History Connection or accepting that the event may simply be undocumented.

# 🏅 Locality Research Guide — California, 1848–1870 (Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdictional Context

California became the 31st U.S. state on **September 9, 1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely — a direct result of the population explosion triggered by the Gold Rush. Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill on **January 24, 1848**, drawing an estimated 300,000 migrants from across the United States and the world. The state's original 27 counties were all established at statehood; additional counties were carved from them through the 1850s–1860s.

The **primary mining counties** most relevant to Gold Rush research are:

| County | Key Mining Areas |
|---|---|
| El Dorado | Coloma (Sutter's Mill), Placerville |
| Placer | Auburn, Rocklin |
| Nevada | Grass Valley, Nevada City |
| Tuolumne | Sonora, Columbia |
| Calaveras | Angels Camp, Mokelumne Hill |
| Amador | Jackson, Sutter Creek |
| Mariposa | Mariposa, Hornitos |
| Trinity / Shasta | Northern diggings |

> **Research quirk:** Miners were often highly transient, moving between counties seasonally. Search multiple counties — don't assume one county holds all of a miner's records.

---

## Record Types, Availability & Access

### 1. 🔢 California State Census, 1852
**The single most important source for the early 1850s.**
- **FamilySearch volume:** imageGroupNumber `006601001` — 522 images, **88% name-indexed**, full-text searchable
- Covers 1850–1852; fills the critical gap left by partial destruction of the 1850 federal census
- Search at: [FamilySearch Record Search](https://www.familysearch.org/search/)
- **Access level: Indexed + images + full-text ✅**

### 2. 📋 U.S. Federal Census — 1850, 1860, 1870
- The **1850 California federal census was partially destroyed** — some county returns are missing entirely. The 1852 State Census is the primary substitute.
- The **1860 and 1870 censuses** survive more completely and are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Mortality schedules** (listing deaths in the prior year) exist for 1850–1885 and are useful for identifying miners who died during or after the rush.
- **Access level: Indexed + images ✅ (1860, 1870); Coverage gap for 1850 ⚠️**

### 3. ⛏️ Mining Claim Registers, 1849–1855
- **FamilySearch volume:** imageGroupNumber `006601002` — 340 images, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**
- Covers San Francisco, California area for 1849–1855
- Must be **browsed image by image** — no name search available
- County recorders' offices also hold mining claim records locally (especially El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras counties)
- **Access level: Browse-only images ⚠️ — must be searched page by page**

### 4. 🚢 Port Arrival Registers / Ship Passenger Manifests, 1849–1858
- **FamilySearch volume:** imageGroupNumber `006601003` — 298 images, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**, Sacramento area
- Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco are held at the **National Archives, San Bruno (NARA Pacific Sierra Region)**; many are also indexed at Ancestry.com
- The wiki notes ([California Genealogy — Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)) that these are a key source: the great majority of '49ers arrived by sea around Cape Horn or via the Isthmus of Panama
- **Access level: Browse-only (FamilySearch volume) ⚠️; Indexed versions on Ancestry ✅**

### 5. 🗳️ California Great Registers, 1866–1910
- **FamilySearch collection 1923340** — 1,345,678 records, 672,839 images
- Voter registration records; include **name, age, occupation, physical description, birthplace/nativity** — the closest thing to a statewide personal profile
- Begin in **1866** (outside the 1850s window, but essential for men who arrived in the Rush and settled permanently)
- [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340)
- **Access level: Indexed + images ✅**

### 6. 👶 County Birth Records, 1850–1919
- **FamilySearch collection 2017276** — 789,456 records, 394,728 images
- [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276)
- **Critical quirk:** California did not mandate **county-level** birth registration until July 1905. Records from the 1850s are very sparse — primarily reflecting births registered voluntarily or by physicians in larger towns.
- **Access level: Indexed + images ✅ — but expect very low coverage for the 1850s**

### 7. 💍 County Marriage Records, 1850–1952
- **FamilySearch collection 1452832** — 567,890 records, 283,945 images
- [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832)
- County clerks recorded marriages from statehood (1850) onward; coverage is better than births for this early period
- **Access level: Indexed + images ✅**

### 8. ⛪ Mission Records, 1769–1850
- **FamilySearch collection 1804372** — 98,765 records, 49,382 images
- Franciscan mission records: baptisms, marriages, burials — primarily for Native Californians and Californio (Spanish/Mexican) families
- Written in **Spanish** — researcher must read or translate the originals
- Pre-dates the Gold Rush but essential for families already resident in California before 1848
- **Access level: Indexed + images ✅ — non-English (Spanish) ⚠️**

### 9. 🪖 Military Records
- Mexican-American War veterans (many enlisted men later joined the Gold Rush)
- California state militia records
- Held at **NARA** and accessible via **[Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)**
- **Access level: Indexed + images on Fold3 ✅**

### 10. 🪦 Cemetery Records
- **[Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/)** covers many Gold Rush-era cemeteries, including historic mining camp burial grounds
- Many small miners' cemeteries were abandoned — local historical societies may have transcriptions
- **Access level: Partially indexed online ✅; physical cemeteries require local contact ⚠️**

### 11. 📰 Historical Newspapers
- **[Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)** holds California newspapers from this era, including the *Alta California* (San Francisco) and various county papers
- Notices of deaths, arrivals, mining discoveries, and legal notices frequently named individuals
- **Access level: Full-text searchable (subscription) ✅**

### 12. 🏛️ Land Records
- Federal land patents: **BLM General Land Office (GLO)** — search free at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov/)
- County deeds: held at individual county recorders' offices; some digitized on FamilySearch or Ancestry
- Mining claims were recorded with county recorders — check each county separately
- **Access level: GLO patents indexed online ✅; county deeds vary ⚠️**

### 13. 🏛️ Naturalization Records
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could occur in **any court of record** — state, county, federal
- California county court records may include declarations of intention ("first papers") and final petitions
- NARA San Bruno holds federal district court naturalizations
- **Access level: Partially indexed; often physical-only at county courthouses ⚠️**

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch.org** | State census 1852, county births/marriages, Great Registers, mission records, mining claim volumes | Free online |
| **National Archives — San Bruno, CA** (NARA Pacific Sierra Region) | Ship passenger manifests, federal court records, naturalizations, federal land records | In-person + some online via Ancestry/Fold3 |
| **California State Archives, Sacramento** | State government records, some county records on microfilm | In-person; [archives.cdn.sos.ca.gov](https://archives.cdn.sos.ca.gov/) |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | Manuscript collections, Gold Rush diaries, newspapers, county histories | In-person; some digitized |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | The preeminent Gold Rush manuscript archive — diaries, letters, land grant papers, Californio collections | In-person (by appointment) |
| **County Courthouses/Recorders** | Mining claims, deeds, probate, marriages, court files — by county | In-person; varies by county |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses, ship passenger lists, newspapers, military records | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service records, pension files | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical California newspapers, *Alta California* | Subscription |
| **BLM GLO** | Federal land patents | Free at glorecords.blm.gov |

---

## Critical Research Quirks

1. **The 1850 federal census is partially destroyed.** Use the **1852 California State Census** (FamilySearch, 88% indexed) as the primary substitute for the early 1850s. This is the single most valuable name-index for placing an ancestor in California in that window.

2. **County-level birth registration was not required until 1905.** For the 1850s, do not expect to find birth records — rely instead on the state census, church registers, and family Bibles.

3. **Most '49ers arrived by sea.** Check ship passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno and on Ancestry.com — many arrivals traveled around Cape Horn or via the Isthmus of Panama and are documented in San Francisco port records.

4. **Mining claim records are browse-only** (FamilySearch imageGroupNumber `006601002`). Budget time to page through them image by image, or contact the county recorder for the specific county where your ancestor mined.

5. **Great Registers begin in 1866**, not the 1850s — but they are the best statewide personal profile record for men who arrived during the Rush and remained. Always check them even when researching an 1850s arrival.

6. **The mining population was extraordinarily diverse.** Chinese, Chilean, Mexican, French, German, and Australian miners all appear in these records; some documents are in non-English languages. The Bancroft Library and California State Library hold significant non-English manuscript collections.

7. **Overland trail records.** Migrants who came overland may appear in trail diaries, emigrant guides, and Missouri River crossing records before they ever arrived in California — start the paper trail in their state of origin.

8. **Mission records are in Spanish** and primarily document pre-Gold Rush Californio families and Native converts. Useful for establishing families already present before 1848, but require translation.

---

## Recommended Research Strategy for a Gold Rush Ancestor

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census** (FamilySearch, 88% indexed) — the best early-decade locator
2. **Search the 1860 and 1870 federal censuses** to track settlement and family formation
3. **Check ship passenger manifests** at NARA San Bruno / Ancestry if sea arrival is possible
4. **Search county marriage records** (FamilySearch collection 1452832) and mining claim registers at the relevant county recorder
5. **Pull the Great Register entry** (FamilySearch collection 1923340) for the 1866+ period
6. **Search Newspapers.com** for the *Alta California* and county papers for death notices, legal notices, or news mentions
7. **Contact the Bancroft Library** for manuscript diaries, letters, or land papers — especially valuable for prominent or well-documented individuals

---

# Locality Research Guide
## New York City — Colonial Period (1700s)
### Jurisdiction: New York Province (British) / New York County

---

## Jurisdictional Context

The 1700s in New York City fall entirely within the **British colonial period (1664–1783)**. The city operated as the administrative capital of **New York Province** under Crown authority. For genealogical purposes, note these critical boundaries:

- **Pre-1664 Dutch origins**: Families with Dutch surnames may have roots in the earlier New Amsterdam period; Dutch-language records survive.
- **1700–1776**: British colonial rule; records generated by provincial courts, Crown-appointed officials, and both Anglican and Dutch Reformed churches.
- **1776–1783**: British military occupation during the Revolutionary War — recordkeeping was disrupted; some residents fled as Loyalists or Patriots.
- **The "State of New York" did not exist until 1777**, and the modern five-borough city structure not until 1898. Colonial NYC was effectively **Manhattan Island = New York County**. Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens, Richmond (Staten Island), and the Bronx were separate jurisdictions — if your family was in those areas, their records sit under those respective colonial county authorities, not New York City proper.

> **⚠️ Quirk:** There was **no civil vital registration** of any kind in colonial New York. Births, marriages, and deaths were recorded exclusively by churches. A missing church record is often a dead end for this period.

---

## Record Types & Access

### 1. 🏛️ Church Records — **PRIMARY VITAL SUBSTITUTE**

**The single most important record class for 1700s NYC families.**

- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers** (1639–continuous): The oldest continuous vital series in New York City. FamilySearch holds **one digitized volume** covering **New York City, 1700–1776** (imageGroupNumber `007733180`, 211 images).
  - ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) — must be browsed image by image.
  - ⚠️ **Written in Dutch** — requires ability to read colonial Dutch script.
  - The broader FamilySearch collection **"New York, Church Records, 1640–1940"** (collection ID [1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)) covers this and related series statewide and is name-indexed.

- **Anglican / Trinity Church**: Trinity Church (founded 1696) on Broadway kept baptismal and burial registers throughout the 1700s. These have been published and are accessible through the **New-York Historical Society** and **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)**.

- **Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Huguenot, Jewish, and Quaker** congregations also maintained registers. The city's diverse immigrant population means denominational affiliation is critical — identify the family's likely religion before searching.

> **Repositories**: FamilySearch ([collection 1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)), New-York Historical Society (N-YHS), NYGBS, individual denominational archives.

---

### 2. ⚖️ Probate Records — **WELL PRESERVED; HIGH PRIORITY**

Colonial New York probate was handled by the **Prerogative Court of New York** (under the Governor/Crown), not a county Surrogate's Court. Wills and estate administrations were filed centrally.

- The **New-York Historical Society** published *Abstracts of Wills* — an indexed series covering colonial-era wills. This is a key finding aid.
- FamilySearch collection **"New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971"** ([collection 1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)) covers colonial-era wills and is the place to begin online.
- The **New York State Archives (NYSA)** holds the original colonial probate files.

> Probate records name heirs, spouses, witnesses, and sometimes ages — invaluable for reconstructing family structure when church records are missing.

---

### 3. 🗺️ Land Records — **GOOD SURVIVAL**

Colonial land was granted by royal patent and recorded through the provincial government.

- FamilySearch collection **"New York, Land Records, 1630–1975"** ([collection 2078654](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654)) covers the colonial period.
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** (held at the New York State Archives) include land patents, grants, and conveyances — a critical series named explicitly in the FamilySearch wiki. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- Land conveyances (deeds) provide names, neighbors, and geographic placement within the city's wards.

---

### 4. 🏛️ Court Records — **Mayor's Court & Colonial Courts**

The **Mayor's Court of New York City** was the primary civil court for Manhattan residents throughout the 1700s. Its records include civil suits, debt actions, and other proceedings that frequently name individuals and relationships.

- Held at the **New York City Municipal Archives** and the **New York State Archives**.
- The FamilySearch wiki specifically names Mayor's Court records as a key colonial source. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

---

### 5. 📋 Tax & Militia Records

- **Tax assessment lists** survive for some years and wards of colonial New York City — these document residents who owned taxable property and are useful for placing families geographically within the city's ward structure. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- **Militia rolls** list men of military age and are a useful supplement for identifying residents who left no church or probate record. ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- Both are held primarily at the **New York State Archives** and have been partially published by genealogical societies.

---

### 6. 📰 Newspapers

- The **New York Gazette** (founded 1725) is the city's earliest newspaper and carried legal notices, death notices, and runaway servant/slave advertisements that name individuals.
- **Newspapers.com** holds historical newspapers; some colonial-era New York papers are accessible there.
- The **New-York Historical Society** and **New York Public Library** hold physical runs.

---

### 7. 📜 Census — CONTEXT NOTE

- There is **no federal census for the colonial period**. The first U.S. federal census is 1790 — post-colonial, but covering the same families one generation later.
- **Colonial enumeration lists** (non-standardized counts ordered by the provincial government at various points) exist for some years and are held at the NYSA.
- The 1790 federal census is the earliest standardized name list and is a logical starting point for working backward into the 1700s.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings for Colonial NYC | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **New York State Archives (NYSA)** | Colonial Manuscripts, land patents, court records, militia/tax lists | Albany, NY; some online via [archives.nysed.gov](https://archives.nysed.gov) |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** | Church transcriptions, published genealogies, colonial vital indexes | NYC + [newyorkfamilyhistory.org](https://www.newyorkfamilyhistory.org) |
| **New-York Historical Society (N-YHS)** | Church registers, Abstracts of Wills, colonial manuscripts | NYC + [nyhistory.org](https://www.nyhistory.org) |
| **New York City Municipal Archives** | City administrative records, Mayor's Court | NYC + some online via [nyc.gov/records](https://www.nyc.gov/site/records) |
| **FamilySearch** | Church records, land, probate (collections above) | Free at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Many NYC colonial collections digitized | Subscription |
| **NARA (National Archives)** | Post-1789 federal records; Revolutionary War pension files | Free via [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) / [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) |

---

## FamilySearch Collections Confirmed for This Period

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| New York, Church Records, 1640–1940 | [1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) | 1640–1940 | Indexed; covers Dutch Reformed, Anglican, others |
| New York, Land Records, 1630–1975 | [2078654](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) | 1630–1975 | Includes colonial patents and conveyances |
| New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971 | [1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) | 1629–1971 | Colonial-era wills and administrations |

*Note: "New York, County Marriages, 1847–1936" and "Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799–1804" fall outside or just at the edge of the 1700s window and are not primary sources for this period.*

---

## Digitized Volume on FamilySearch

| Volume | Image Group | Years | Record Type | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dutch Reformed Church Registers | `007733180` | 1700–1776 | Baptisms, marriages, burials | ⚠️ Browse-only; 0% indexed; **Dutch language** |

---

## Key Quirks & Researcher Warnings

1. **No civil registration**: Church records are the only vital-event series for the 1700s. Identify the denomination first.
2. **Dutch-language records**: Dutch Reformed registers on FamilySearch must be browsed image-by-image and read in colonial Dutch. Consider a translator or transcription service.
3. **Colonial vs. state jurisdiction split**: Records before 1777 are filed under colonial provincial authority (Prerogative Court for probate, provincial land office for patents), not the later county-level courts that took over after statehood.
4. **"New York City" in the 1700s = Manhattan only**: Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens, Richmond (Staten Island), and Westchester/Bronx records are under separate colonial county jurisdictions — search those separately if your family was outside Manhattan.
5. **British occupation (1776–1783)**: The Revolutionary War period saw population displacement, record disruption, and Loyalist emigration. Some families who left as Loyalists have records in Nova Scotia or Ontario archives.
6. **The 1790 federal census** is the earliest name-by-name federal enumeration — start there and work backward using church and probate records into the 1700s.
7. **FamilySearch wiki place pages** for New York City and New York State returned only a generic fallback — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy) for the full NYC-specific research article.

---

## Recommended Starting Strategy

1. **Identify the denomination** of your ancestor's family (Dutch Reformed, Anglican, Presbyterian, etc.)
2. Search **FamilySearch collection 1469062** (Church Records) for baptism/marriage/burial records
3. Run **probate records** (collection 1542780) for any adult males who may have left wills
4. Search **land records** (collection 2078654) to place the family geographically within a ward
5. Check the **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** ([newyorkfamilyhistory.org](https://www.newyorkfamilyhistory.org)) — they have published and indexed many colonial NYC records not yet on FamilySearch
6. If Dutch Reformed ancestry is likely, browse the **Dutch-language volume** (`007733180`) on FamilySearch directly, or contact the NYGBS for transcription assistance

---

# Virginia — Revolutionary War Era Locality Guide
**Target period:** 1775–1783 | **Focus:** Military service & wartime activities
**Standard place:** Virginia, United States

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies and maintained **county-level** record-keeping from the 1630s — one of the best-documented colonial jurisdictions in North America (Wikipedia: [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)). During the Revolution, Virginia was organized entirely into counties; there was **no statewide vital registration** (that did not begin until 1853). Records of births, marriages, and deaths for this period survive, if at all, through **county Anglican vestry books and church registers**.

Two critical structural facts govern research in this period:

1. **The 1790 Virginia federal census is missing.** It was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The 1782–1785 **personal property tax lists** are the primary population substitute and are indispensable for identifying households during and immediately after the Revolution.
2. Virginia contributed **more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony**, and it administered its own parallel militia and state navy. Military records therefore come from *both* federal (NARA) and state (Library of Virginia) repositories — you must search both.

---

## Record Classes & Access

### 🎖️ 1. Military Service Records — Continental Line
- **What:** Compiled military service records and muster rolls for Virginia soldiers in the Continental Army.
- **Repository:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), **Record Group 93**.
- **Online access:** [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) — digitized NARA Revolutionary War compiled military service records are keyword- and name-searchable here. Also available via [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/).
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783** (Collection ID [1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)) — 345,678 indexed records with images (name-indexed; searchable by name on FamilySearch).
- **Access level:** ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch & Fold3)

### 🏡 2. Virginia Militia Records
- **What:** Muster rolls, pay vouchers, and officer lists for Virginia state militia forces — a separate body from the Continental Line.
- **Repository:** **Library of Virginia**, Richmond, VA ([lva.virginia.gov](https://www.lva.virginia.gov)).
- **Online access:** Partial digitization through the Library of Virginia's online catalog and digital collections. Check their "Revolutionary War Records" finding aid.
- **Access level:** ⚠️ Physical + partial online; browse the Library of Virginia catalog before planning an in-person visit.

### 🪙 3. Revolutionary War Pension & Bounty Land Warrant Files
- **What:** Applications filed by veterans (or their widows) for federal pensions and bounty land — among the **richest genealogical records** of the period. Files often contain detailed service narratives, family relationships, ages, and county of residence.
- **Repository:** NARA, **Record Group 15**. The applications are indexed and digitized.
- **Online access:** [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) — fully digitized and name-indexed. Also via Ancestry.com's "U.S. Revolutionary War Pension and Bounty-Land Warrant Application Files" database.
- **Access level:** ✅ Indexed + images (Fold3 / Ancestry)
- **Quirk:** Widows' pension applications, filed decades later, often contain marriage dates, death dates, and children's names absent from any other source — always search for the widow's application, not just the veteran's.

### 🌾 4. Virginia Military District of Ohio — Bounty Land Warrants & Surveys
- **What:** Virginia reserved a tract in present-day Ohio (the "Virginia Military District") to fulfill bounty-land promises to its Revolutionary War veterans. Warrant and survey records connect veterans to specific service claims.
- **Repository:** **Library of Virginia** (warrant files) and the **Ohio History Connection** (survey plats). NARA also holds related records.
- **Online access:** BLM General Land Office Records ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) for patent records. Library of Virginia has warrant records online.
- **Access level:** ⚠️ Partial online — warrants searchable, survey plats may require correspondence.

### 📋 5. Personal Property Tax Lists, 1782–1850
- **What:** Annual county-level lists of taxable males (21+) and their property. The 1782–1785 lists are the **critical substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia census** and establish who was living in each county during and just after the war.
- **Repository:** Library of Virginia (originals); FamilySearch microfilm.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850** (Collection ID [1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723)) — 456,789 indexed records with 228,394 images.
- **Access level:** ✅ Indexed + images
- **Quirk:** Men absent on military service may be listed with reduced or deferred taxes — absence from a tax list during 1775–1783 can itself be evidence of active service away from home.

### ⛪ 6. Church Records (Anglican / Episcopal Vestry Books)
- **What:** The Church of England (later Episcopal Church) was the established church of colonial Virginia. Vestry books recorded baptisms, marriages, burials, and poor-relief — the closest equivalent to civil vital registration before 1853.
- **Repository:** Many vestry books are at the Library of Virginia; others remain with individual parishes or the Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929** (Collection ID [1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)) — 1,234,567 indexed records with 617,283 images.
- **Access level:** ✅ Indexed + images (on FamilySearch)
- **Quirk:** Dissenting congregations (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian) grew rapidly during the Revolution as the Anglican church lost state support. If your ancestor was not Anglican, check FamilySearch for separate Baptist or Methodist register microfilms for Virginia, or contact the respective denominational archives.

### 📜 7. Land, Marriage & Will Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900** (Collection ID [1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)) — 2,567,890 indexed records with 1,283,945 images.
- **What's included:** County deed books, marriage bonds and registers, and will books. Wartime land transactions, estate settlements of soldiers who died in service, and marriage bonds of young men before deployment can all be found here.
- **Access level:** ✅ Indexed + images

### ⚖️ 8. County Court Order Books
- **What:** Virginia county courts met quarterly and recorded a wide range of wartime civil activity: appointment of militia officers, loyalty oaths, supply contracts, road and ferry maintenance, orphan guardianships (for children of soldiers who died), and writs of impressment.
- **Repository:** County courthouses (originals); Library of Virginia (many microfilmed).
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920** (Collection ID [2134567](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567)) — 1,789,012 indexed records with 894,506 images.
- **Access level:** ✅ Indexed + images

### 📰 9. Historical Newspapers
- **What:** The *Virginia Gazette* (Williamsburg, later Richmond, 1736s–1780s) published muster calls, lists of deserters, officer commissions, casualty notices, and estate notices for soldiers.
- **Online access:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) — some Virginia colonial/Revolutionary-era newspapers digitized. Also check **Chronicling America** ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)) for free access.
- **Access level:** ⚠️ Partial — coverage is incomplete for the 1775–1783 window; browse by date.

### 🪦 10. Cemetery Records
- **What:** Many Revolutionary War veteran graves in Virginia were marked by the Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) and are documented with headstone photos.
- **Online access:** [FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) — free and name-searchable.
- **Access level:** ✅ Searchable (user-submitted; coverage varies by county)

---

## Repository Directory

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA** (Washington, DC / St. Louis) | RG 93 (Continental service records), RG 15 (pensions & bounty land warrants) | Online via Fold3 & Ancestry; in-person at NARA facilities |
| **Library of Virginia**, Richmond | Virginia militia, tax lists, vestry books, county records microfilm, VMD-Ohio warrants | [lva.virginia.gov](https://www.lva.virginia.gov); in-person & some online |
| **FamilySearch.org** | 5 digitized Virginia collections (see above) spanning church, military, tax, land, and court records | Free online; name-indexed |
| **Fold3.com** | Digitized NARA Revolutionary War compiled service records; pension files | Subscription; name-searchable |
| **Ancestry.com** | Pension files, census, land; U.S. military databases | Subscription |
| **Virginia Historical Society** (now Virginia Museum of History & Culture) | Family papers, correspondence, officer diaries | In-person; some finding aids online at [virginiahistory.org](https://www.virginiahistory.org) |
| **DAR Library**, Washington, DC | Lineage papers, compiled rosters, published county histories | [dar.org/library](https://www.dar.org/library); partially online |
| **FindAGrave.com** | Headstone photos, grave locations (incl. DAR-marked veteran graves) | Free online |

---

## Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **The 1790 Virginia federal census is gone.** Always begin with the 1782–1785 personal property tax lists as your population baseline. These are indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1456723).
2. **Search both NARA (Continental) and Library of Virginia (militia).** A man could have served in both — or only in the militia — and the records do not overlap.
3. **Always search for a widow's pension file**, not just the veteran's. Widows' applications were filed years or decades later and routinely include marriage dates, children's names, and death information not found elsewhere.
4. **Virginia Military District of Ohio warrants** link a Virginia ancestor to a specific service claim even when service records are sparse — search these if other military records are thin.
5. **County boundaries shifted frequently** in 18th-century Virginia as new counties were carved from older ones. Identify which county your ancestor lived in *at the time of each event* — an ancestor's county in 1775 may differ from their county in 1783. The Library of Virginia's "Virginia County Formation" resource lists parent counties and formation dates.
6. **Absence from a tax list during 1775–1783** may indicate active military service away from home — it is not necessarily a gap in records.
7. **Dissenting-church records** (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian) are not fully consolidated; seek them through denominational archives in addition to FamilySearch.
8. **No statewide vital registration until 1853.** Church records and county registers are the only sources for births, marriages, and deaths during this period.

---

## Suggested Search Order

1. **FamilySearch** — Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (Collection 1945678) — free, name-indexed, images
2. **Fold3** — Revolutionary War compiled service records (NARA RG 93) and pension files (RG 15)
3. **FamilySearch** — Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (Collection 1456723) — establish household in county
4. **FamilySearch** — Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (Collection 2134567) — militia appointments, loyalty oaths, guardianships
5. **FamilySearch** — Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (Collection 1734285)
6. **FamilySearch** — Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (Collection 1598230)
7. **Library of Virginia** — militia records, additional tax lists, vestry books not yet digitized
8. **Fold3 / BLM GLO** — Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty land warrants and surveys
9. **Newspapers.com / Chronicling America** — Virginia Gazette and other period newspapers
10. **FindAGrave** — cemetery and DAR-marked grave records
