# Locality Research Guide
## Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Industry
*Target period: c. 1865–1910 | Controlling jurisdiction: Allegheny County (est. 1788)*

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Allegheny County** was formed in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties; Pittsburgh is the county seat. Almost all civil records for Pittsburgh-area families are filed at the **county level**, not the city level.

**Critical boundary note — Allegheny City:** During the entire target period, the city of Allegheny (today Pittsburgh's North Side) was a separate municipality across the Allegheny River. It was not annexed by Pittsburgh until **1907**. Families living in that area before 1907 appear in records under **"Allegheny City"** or **"Allegheny, Pennsylvania"** — not Pittsburgh. Always search both place names for the late 19th century.

**1890 Census loss:** The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire. For families in Pittsburgh during that decade, substitute sources are essential (see below).

---

### 1. 🏭 Occupational & Industrial Records *(Primary focus)*

These are the specialty sources for steel-era research and are **not available through FamilySearch** — they require direct repository contact.

| Source | What It Documents | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Company employment records | Hire dates, wages, departments, sometimes birthplace & next-of-kin | **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh); **Rivers of Steel Archives** (Homestead, PA) | Physical access; fragmentary survival |
| Union membership lists | AAISW (Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel & Tin Workers) member rolls | Heinz History Center; Library of Congress | Physical/microfilm; some digitized |
| City directories | Occupation, home address, employer; published annually | **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** (complete run from 1813) | In-person and partial digitization on Ancestry.com |
| State factory inspector reports | Worker counts by mill, working conditions, accident records | **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Physical access |
| Federal census occupation columns | Occupation listed for every person | FamilySearch; Ancestry.com | Indexed + images |

> ⚠️ **Coverage gap:** Corporate consolidations, closures, and the industry's turbulent history mean many company employment records did not survive. The absence of a record is not proof of non-employment. Treat surviving records as a bonus, not a baseline.

**Key repositories for industrial research:**
- **Heinz History Center** — 1212 Smallman St, Pittsburgh, PA 15222. The single most important repository for Pittsburgh industrial and immigration records.
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area Archives** — 623 E. Waterfront Dr, Homestead, PA 15120. Focused on the steel mill communities of the Monongahela Valley.

---

### 2. 📋 Federal Census Records

The census is your best comprehensive occupational snapshot for the target period.

| Year | Value for Steel Research | Access |
|---|---|---|
| 1870 | Occupation listed; large immigrant workforce visible | FamilySearch (indexed); Ancestry |
| 1880 | Occupation + birthplace of both parents; most immigrants now established | FamilySearch (free, indexed); Ancestry |
| **1890** | **⚠️ Nearly entirely destroyed by fire** | Substitute: city directories, church records, state veterans schedules |
| 1900 | Occupation + **immigration year** + years in US; essential for timing arrivals | Ancestry (indexed); FamilySearch |
| 1910 | Occupation + employer type; captures post-Homestead Strike workforce | Ancestry (indexed); FamilySearch |

Federal census records for Allegheny County survive from 1800. The **1880 and 1900 schedules** are the most valuable enumerations for tracing industrial workers in the target period.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))*

---

### 3. 📜 Vital Records

Pennsylvania did **not** mandate statewide registration of births and deaths until **1906**. However, Allegheny County began recording births and deaths at the **county level from 1870** — more than 35 years before the statewide mandate. Search county records first for events between 1870 and 1905.

| Record Type | Date Range | FamilySearch Collection | Records | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Death certificates (statewide) | 1906–1968 | [Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) (ID: 2255317) | 4,218,763 | Indexed + images |
| County marriages | 1885–1950 | [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) (ID: 1921317) | 524,189 | Indexed + images |
| Civil marriages | 1677–1950 | [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) (ID: 1571957) | 312,045 | Indexed + images |
| Compiled marriages | 1700–1900 | [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) (ID: 1502909) | 198,765 | Indexed — **no images** |

> ⚠️ County-level birth/death registration (1870–1905) is held at the **Allegheny County Health Department** and the **Pennsylvania State Archives** — these records are not fully digitized on FamilySearch. Marriage licenses from 1885 are at the **Allegheny County Courthouse**.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))*

---

### 4. ⛪ Church Records *(Critical for immigrant steel workers)*

For the waves of Catholic immigrants who staffed the mills, **ethnic parish registers are often the only family record source** — predating or paralleling civil registration and recording baptisms, marriages, and burials in rich detail.

| Collection | Date Range | FamilySearch ID | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638) | 1708–1985 | 1401638 | 1,245,830 | Indexed + images |

**Ethnic parishes to target by community:**
- **Slovak** — St. Gabriel, St. Matthew, St. Wendelin (Braddock), Holy Trinity
- **Polish** — St. Stanislaus Kostka, Sacred Heart of Jesus
- **Croatian** — St. Nicholas Croatian Catholic
- **Italian** — St. Peter, Immaculate Heart of Mary
- **Irish** — St. Patrick, St. Paul Cathedral
- **German** — St. Mary of Mercy, Holy Trinity Lutheran

> 🔑 **Parish records are frequently in the immigrant language** (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, German). Plan for translation. Original registers are held by the **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** and individual parishes. Many are also on FamilySearch microfilm.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))*

---

### 5. 🚢 Naturalization & Immigration Records

The steel boom drew massive immigrant waves. Naturalization is a two-step process with distinct record sets:

| Record | Date Range | Repository | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalizations | 1798–1930 | **National Archives at Philadelphia** (NARA mid-Atlantic) | Pre-1906 records can appear in any court of record |
| Federal court naturalizations | Post-1906 | NARA Philadelphia | After 1906, all naturalizations go through federal courts only |
| Passenger arrival lists | 1820s–1950s | NARA; Ancestry.com; FamilySearch | Most Pittsburgh immigrants arrived through NYC, Baltimore, or Philadelphia |

> ⚠️ Pre-1906 naturalization records can be filed in **any court of record** — federal, state, or local. The Allegheny County series is the primary local repository but is not exhaustive. Also check Allegheny County Quarter Sessions court records.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))*

---

### 6. 🏛 Probate Records

| Collection | Date Range | FamilySearch ID | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 1683–1994 | 1999196 | 893,214 | Indexed + images |

Probate files can name heirs, creditors, and business partners — useful for establishing family relationships and economic standing within the mill community.

---

### 7. 📰 Newspapers & Directories

| Source | Value | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Pittsburgh city directories | Annual; list occupation, address, employer | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (1813–present); Ancestry.com (partial) |
| *Pittsburgh Gazette*, *Post-Gazette*, *Dispatch* | Vital notices, labor strikes, accident reports, immigrant community news | Newspapers.com; Carnegie Library microfilm |
| Ethnic-language newspapers | Community news, obituaries in immigrant languages | Carnegie Library; various ethnic archives |

Strike coverage (especially the **1892 Homestead Strike** and surrounding labor actions) can document individual workers and their roles.

---

### 8. ⚰️ Cemetery & Death Records

| Source | Repository |
|---|---|
| Cemetery records | FindAGrave.com; BillionGraves |
| Allegheny County death registers (1870–1905) | Pennsylvania State Archives; Allegheny County Health Dept. |
| Statewide death certificates (1906+) | FamilySearch collection 2255317 (indexed + images) |

Major Pittsburgh cemeteries of the period: Allegheny Cemetery, St. Mary's Cemetery (Lawrenceville), Calvary Catholic Cemetery, Union Dale Cemetery.

---

### 9. 🏗 Military Records

Many steel workers were Civil War veterans who came to Pittsburgh for postwar industrial work.

| Source | Repository |
|---|---|
| Civil War service & pension records | NARA (Fold3; Ancestry.com) |
| Pennsylvania regimental histories | Pennsylvania State Archives |
| Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) posts | Heinz History Center; local posts' records |
| WWI draft registration cards (1917–18) | NARA; Ancestry.com (digitized) — useful for workers present at the tail end of the period |

---

### 10. 🔗 Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Focus | Location / URL |
|---|---|---|
| **Heinz History Center** | Industrial, immigration, city records | Pittsburgh, PA — [heinzhistorycenter.org](https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org) |
| **Rivers of Steel Archives** | Steel mill employment & community records | Homestead, PA |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories, local newspapers, local history | Pittsburgh, PA — [carnegielibrary.org](https://www.carnegielibrary.org) |
| **National Archives — Philadelphia** | Naturalization (1798–1930), passenger lists | Philadelphia, PA — [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) |
| **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Ethnic parish registers | Pittsburgh, PA |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** | Statewide records, factory reports | Harrisburg, PA — [phmc.pa.gov](https://www.phmc.pa.gov) |
| **FamilySearch.org** | 6 Pennsylvania digitized collections | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, city directories, immigration | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Pittsburgh newspapers | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military records | Subscription |

---

### ⚠️ Key Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Allegheny City ≠ Pittsburgh before 1907.** Families in today's North Side appear in records as residents of *Allegheny City* — always search both city names for the target period.
2. **County birth/death registration began 1870**, not 1906 — search county-level records for events between 1870 and 1905, held at the Allegheny County Health Department and Pennsylvania State Archives.
3. **The 1890 federal census is almost entirely gone.** Substitute with city directories (annual), church records, county tax lists, and Pennsylvania veterans schedules.
4. **Company employment records are fragmentary.** Do not assume non-employment if no record is found — survivorship of these records is the exception, not the rule.
5. **Ethnic parish registers are in the immigrant language.** Slovak, Polish, Croatian, and Italian registers require translation.
6. **Pre-1906 naturalizations can be in any court.** Don't limit to federal court — check the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas series (1798–1930) at NARA Philadelphia.
7. **Allegheny County is the filing unit, not Pittsburgh city.** All county-level records (marriage licenses, probate, deeds, naturalizations) are filed by county, not by city ward or neighborhood.

# Locality Research Guide
## Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — Families Affected by the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Philadelphia County was established in **1682** when William Penn founded the colony. In 1793, Philadelphia was simultaneously the county seat, the state capital, and the national capital. At this date, **Philadelphia City and Philadelphia County were legally separate jurisdictions** — both coexisted within the same boundaries. They remained separate until the **Act of Consolidation (1854)**, which merged all Philadelphia County municipalities into one city. For 1793 research, records may be filed under either "Philadelphia City" or "Philadelphia County" — check both.

The yellow fever epidemic struck Philadelphia from **August to November 1793**, killing approximately **5,000 of the city's 50,000 residents** — roughly one-tenth of the population. Tens of thousands more fled, dispersing to surrounding counties (Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, and Bucks). This dual impact — mass death *and* mass displacement — shapes where records of affected families will be found.

**Critical baseline:** Pennsylvania did **not** have statewide vital registration in 1793. Statewide death registration did not begin until **1906** ([FamilySearch Wiki — Philadelphia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)). Church registers are therefore the **only** systematic vital record source for this period. Every death or burial in 1793 was recorded (if at all) by a congregation, not a government office.

---

### Epidemic-Specific Records

These sources exist *because* of the 1793 outbreak and are the most direct for identifying affected families.

#### 1. Mathew Carey's Published Death List
Carey's pamphlet *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793, with later editions) contains one of the only contemporary name lists of epidemic dead. It was reprinted multiple times and is widely held by research libraries. **Access:** Available in digitized form through HathiTrust and Google Books; physical copies at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) and the Library Company of Philadelphia.

#### 2. Committee of Citizens — Minutes and Reports
A committee was appointed by the city's citizens to coordinate relief and document the crisis. Their minutes and reports name individuals who received aid, were treated, or died. These are **manuscript sources** held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** (HSP), 1300 Locust Street, Philadelphia. Not digitized or name-indexed on FamilySearch.

#### 3. Bush Hill Hospital Records
Bush Hill was the city's improvised epidemic hospital. Its patient and death records, where they survive, are manuscript materials at HSP. Coverage is incomplete — not all patients were formally registered.

#### 4. Philadelphia City Archives
The Philadelphia City Archives (City Hall Annex, 3101 Market Street) holds **municipal administration records** from the epidemic period, including some Committee correspondence and official city documents. Not digitized for this period; physical visit or written inquiry required.

---

### Church Records ⭐ Primary Source Tier

Church records are the **essential substitute for absent civil registration** throughout this period. Philadelphia's exceptional religious diversity means each denomination maintained its own registers — you must identify which congregation your family belonged to.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985* (Collection ID: 1401638) — **1,245,830 records**, with images. Covers baptisms, marriages, and burials across multiple denominations for the epidemic period. Searchable at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638).

Key congregations active in Philadelphia in 1793, many with surviving burial registers:

| Congregation | Affiliation | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Christ Church | Anglican/Episcopal | One of the largest congregations; burial registers survive and are partially indexed |
| Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church) | Lutheran/Episcopal | Oldest church in Pennsylvania; registers survive from 1697 |
| St. Peter's Church | Episcopal | Shared burial ground with Christ Church |
| St. Paul's Church | Episcopal | Active in epidemic period |
| First Presbyterian Church | Presbyterian | Registers held by Presbyterian Historical Society |
| Second Presbyterian | Presbyterian | — |
| Mikveh Israel | Jewish | Burial records at the congregation's archives |
| Friends (Quakers) | Society of Friends | Highly organized meeting records; Friends were leaders in epidemic relief |
| St. Mary's / St. Joseph's | Roman Catholic | Earliest Catholic parishes in the city |
| German Reformed | Reformed | Served the German immigrant community |
| German Lutheran | Lutheran | — |

**Manuscript originals and transcriptions** for many of these congregations are held at HSP. The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** (GSP) has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records — consult their published *Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine* and their database at [genpa.org](https://www.genpa.org).

**Presbyterian Historical Society** (425 Lombard Street, Philadelphia) holds Presbyterian church registers. **Friends Historical Library** (Swarthmore College) and the **Quaker & Special Collections at Haverford College** hold Friends Meeting records.

---

### Probate Records ⭐ High-Priority for Epidemic Deaths

Every estate left by an epidemic victim would generate a probate filing. The **Philadelphia County Orphans' Court** handled wills, administrations, guardianships, and inventories.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* (Collection ID: 1999196) — **893,214 records** with images. Covers the 1793 period. Searchable at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196).

Probate records are especially valuable here because:
- They name the deceased, executor/administrator, heirs, and creditors
- Guardianship filings name orphaned children (epidemic deaths left many)
- Estate inventories describe household goods and economic status
- Administrations were filed when someone died intestate (without a will) — common in sudden epidemic deaths

The **Register of Wills**, Philadelphia, holds original volumes. Many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.

---

### Census Records

| Year | Notes |
|---|---|
| **1790 federal census** | Taken 3 years before the epidemic — establishes who was present in the household before the outbreak. Heads of household only; available on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| **1800 federal census** | Taken 7 years after — reveals surviving household composition and can help infer who was lost |
| **1810 federal census** | Further recovery-period baseline |

There is no Pennsylvania state census for this period. The **1890 federal census was largely destroyed** by fire. Mortality schedules do not begin until 1850. These gaps make the church and probate records above even more critical.

---

### Land, Tax, and Property Records

Philadelphia published **city directories** beginning in 1785 (Francis White's *Philadelphia Directory*) with editions through the epidemic period. Directories list heads of household by name and occupation — a name disappearing from successive directories after 1793 can be strong negative evidence of death or out-migration.

**Pennsylvania tax assessment lists** survive for Philadelphia County for the late 18th century and are held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) and partially microfilmed by FamilySearch. These are browse-only for this period.

**Deed books** (Philadelphia County) document property transfers resulting from estate settlements. Held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and the **Philadelphia Recorder of Deeds**. FamilySearch has microfilmed portions but indexing is sparse for the 1793 period — expect browse-only access.

---

### Newspaper Death Notices

Philadelphia had several active newspapers in 1793 that published death notices throughout the epidemic:
- *Federal Gazette* (published daily epidemic death tallies)
- *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*
- *General Advertiser*

These are **not name-indexed** for genealogical searching. Access via:
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) — [chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) — some Philadelphia titles digitized
- **Newspapers.com** — broader coverage, subscription required
- **HSP and Library Company of Philadelphia** — hold original runs on microfilm

---

### Military Records (Peripheral for 1793)

The 1793 epidemic preceded the War of 1812. For families with Revolutionary War service:
- **Pension files** at NARA name widows and children — a widow's pension filed after an epidemic death would document the family
- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) has Revolutionary War service records and pension files indexed

---

### Out-Migration: Surrounding County Records

Thousands fled Philadelphia during the epidemic. If your family is found in surrounding counties in 1793–1795, check:

| County | Distance | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Montgomery County, PA** | North | Germantown (then a separate borough) received many refugees |
| **Delaware County, PA** | Southwest | — |
| **Chester County, PA** | West | — |
| **Bucks County, PA** | Northeast | — |
| **Burlington County, NJ** | East (across Delaware River) | Some families crossed into New Jersey |

Church and probate records in these counties may document Philadelphia families who fled and either returned, settled permanently, or died there.

### Research Quirks to Know

1. **No civil vital registration in 1793.** Pennsylvania statewide death registration began in 1906. Church burial registers are the *only* systematic source — identify the congregation first.
2. **Philadelphia City and County were separate pre-1854.** Records may be filed under either jurisdiction. The 1854 Act of Consolidation merged them.
3. **Mathew Carey's list is not exhaustive.** It names many dead but does not capture everyone. Cross it against church burial registers.
4. **Out-migration is well-documented.** Thousands fled. If a family disappears from Philadelphia in 1793–1794, check Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, and Bucks County records — and Burlington County, NJ across the river.
5. **Quaker records are unusually rich.** The Society of Friends was deeply involved in epidemic relief and maintained meticulous meeting records. If the family had any Quaker connection, Friends records at Swarthmore and Haverford are high-value.
6. **Orphans' Court is a goldmine.** The epidemic left many orphans. Guardianship filings in the Philadelphia County Orphans' Court name children individually and document family structure — often more than a will does.
7. **Directories as negative evidence.** Compare city directories from 1791–1792 against 1794–1795 editions. A name that vanishes is circumstantial evidence of epidemic death or flight.

# Locality Research Guide
## Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — circa 1871 (Great Chicago Fire)
**Survey period: 1860–1885**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Chicago (incorporated 1833/1837) sits in Cook County, established 1831. By 1870 it was one of America's largest cities and a major immigrant hub. **The Great Chicago Fire burned October 8–10, 1871**, destroyed ~3.3 square miles, killed ~300 people, and left more than 100,000 homeless. Critically for genealogists, **the fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse**, which housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records (including naturalizations), probate files, and tax rolls. Many church registers in the burned district were also lost. *(Wikipedia, [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire))*

**Vital registration levels to keep straight:**
- **County-level** civil registration in Cook County began around 1871
- **Statewide** Illinois civil registration did not begin until **1877**
- Before both of those dates, church records are the primary vital record source — and many were destroyed

---

## ⚠️ What the Fire Destroyed (Pre-October 1871 Gap)

The following are **lost or severely disrupted** for the pre-fire period:
- County deed and property records
- City/county birth and death registers
- Court records at the courthouse (naturalizations, civil suits, guardianships)
- Probate files
- Tax rolls
- Church registers held inside the burn zone

Substitute sources (§3 below) are **essential** for any family events before October 1871.

---

## 1. Surviving Post-Fire Vital Records on FamilySearch

All three collections below are **name-indexed with images** — searchable directly on FamilySearch. Note that records in the very early 1870s may be incomplete due to post-fire administrative disruption.

| Collection | ID | Records | Dates |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County Birth Certificates | 2024189 | 1,450,000 | 1871–1940 |
| Cook County Death Records | 1913456 | 980,000 | 1871–1947 |
| Cook County Marriage Records | 1756321 | 620,000 | 1871–1920 |

---

## 2. Church Records

**FamilySearch Collection**: *Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925* (ID 1803978) — **285,000 indexed records** spanning both pre- and post-fire periods. This is the **primary source for vital events before 1871**, since civil registration either didn't yet exist or was destroyed.

- Parishes **outside the burn zone** often preserved their registers; those inside the burned district did not
- The **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds Catholic parish registers not yet digitized — contact them directly for pre-fire parishes
- Check individual denominational archives (Lutheran synod, Episcopal diocese, Methodist conference) for non-Catholic registers

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories))*

---

## 3. Substitute Sources for the Pre-Fire Period

### Federal Census (Survived — originals held in Washington, D.C.)
The **1870 census** is your single most important surviving pre-fire document — it was enumerated in June 1870, before the fire, and survived because the originals were in Washington. Searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

| Census Year | Status |
|---|---|
| 1850 | Survived |
| 1860 | Survived |
| **1870** | **Survived — the key pre-fire snapshot** |
| 1880 | Post-fire; captures rebuilt population |

**Mortality schedules (1850–1880)** record deaths in the year preceding the census — useful for identifying fire casualties near a census year.

### Reconstructed Property Records — Burnt Record Act (1872)
The Illinois legislature's **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-register their deeds. These re-registrations are the primary substitute for pre-fire property records.

- **FamilySearch Volume DGS 009982111** — *Post-fire Property Re-recordings*, 1871–1880, 112 images, **41% name-indexed** (partially searchable on FamilySearch; remainder must be browsed image-by-image). Not full-text searchable.
- Physical originals also held at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds and at IRAD (see §7)
- ⚠️ Coverage is **incomplete**: families who fled Chicago or died in the fire may not have re-registered

### Pre-Fire Reconstructed Court Records
- **FamilySearch Volume DGS 009982110** — *Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies)*, 1865–1871, 38 images. **Browse-only: 0% indexed, not full-text searchable** — must be examined image-by-image with no search capability. These are post-fire copies, not originals.
- Work DGS 009982110 (1865–1871) and DGS 009982111 (1871–1880) together as one continuous research trail across the fire break.

### Insurance Records — Chicago Title and Trust Company
Insurance records survived the fire and document pre-fire property ownership and occupancy. The **Chicago History Museum** holds the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection, named by the FamilySearch Wiki as a key substitute for pre-fire research. *(Source: [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))*

### City Directories (1840s onward — Survived)
Annual city directories listing residents by name and address survived the fire. They provide year-by-year location evidence both before and after 1871. Held at the **Newberry Library**, Chicago. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, same page)*

### Newspapers
The *Chicago Tribune* and *Chicago Times* continued publishing through and after the fire, reporting lists of the dead, missing, and homeless, plus relief distribution. Access via **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) and the Newberry Library's newspaper collections.

---

## 4. Immigration and Naturalization

Chicago was a major destination for German, Irish, Scandinavian, Polish, and Czech immigrants. Pre-fire naturalizations in Cook County court were destroyed. Strategies:

- **Federal passenger lists** (not locally held — survived): Searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Post-1872 Cook County naturalizations**: IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University
- **U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois**: Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in federal court (records at NARA Great Lakes Region, Chicago) — these were *not* in the county courthouse and were unaffected by the fire
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in *any* court of record — cast a wide net across surviving federal and state court records

---

## 5. Military Records

Many Chicago men were Civil War veterans (1861–1865). Military records are held federally and were **unaffected by the fire**:

- **Compiled Military Service Records and pension files**: NARA, searchable via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)
- **Illinois Adjutant General's records**: Illinois State Archives, Springfield — unaffected by the Chicago fire
- **Pension files are especially valuable** as a post-fire substitute: they contain affidavits from family members, neighbors, and physicians that can reconstruct birth, marriage, and nativity details when local records are gone

---

## 6. Land Records

- **Federal land patents** (BLM General Land Office, glorecords.blm.gov): Original federal grants in Illinois — federal records, unaffected by the fire
- **Post-fire deeds**: Burnt Record Act re-registrations (DGS 009982111, see §3)
- Cook County Recorder of Deeds holds post-fire originals

---

| **Newberry Library**, Chicago | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscript collections, local histories | In-person; some digitized |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance records, fire relief records, photographs, personal papers | In-person research |
| **IRAD — Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County post-fire court and government records | In-person |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago, Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (pre- and post-fire) | Contact archives directly |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 | In-person / online portal |
| **Illinois State Archives**, Springfield | State-level records; unaffected by the Chicago fire | In-person; some digitized |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region**, Chicago | Federal court naturalization records, some military | In-person; some on Fold3/Ancestry |
| **NARA**, Washington/College Park | Federal census originals, military service records, pension files, passenger lists | Fold3, Ancestry, FamilySearch |

## Key Quirks for Great Fire Research

1. **The 1870 federal census is your anchor** — it survived because originals were in Washington. This is the best surviving document placing Chicago families in the months before the disaster.
2. **Statewide Illinois registration began in 1877, not 1871** — pre-fire births, marriages, and deaths depend on church records, many of which were also lost in the burn zone.
3. **Reconstructed records are incomplete** — Burnt Record Act re-registrations only cover families who came forward; those who fled or died may be absent entirely.
4. **Search denomination archives proactively** — parishes outside the burned district preserved registers. Don't rely solely on what FamilySearch has digitized.
5. **Pension files are among the most powerful substitutes** — for veteran households, a pension file can supply birth, marriage, nativity, and neighbor testimony that replaces destroyed local records.
6. **Federal court naturalizations survived the fire** — the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois was not in the Cook County Courthouse; those records are at NARA Great Lakes Region.
7. **Work the two property/court FamilySearch volumes as one trail** — DGS 009982110 (1865–1871, browse-only) and DGS 009982111 (1871–1880, 41% indexed) straddle the fire break and together cover the pre/post transition.

---

The FamilySearch Wiki's Cook County page at **https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy** is the authoritative ongoing reference for this locality — consult it for updates to digitization coverage and any repository access changes.

# Locality Guide: French Colonial Louisiana (1699–1769)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Colonial authority:** France, as an administrative district of New France (1699–1762); ceded to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762), with effective Spanish rule beginning 1769 under Governor O'Reilly
- **Eastern portion:** Ceded to Britain by the Treaty of Paris (1763); researchers with ancestors near Natchez or Mobile should also check British West Florida records
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville)
- **Governing body:** The Superior Council (*Conseil Supérieur*) — the colony's court, legislative, and administrative authority; it created the primary civil record series for this period
- **Administrative divisions:** Not yet organized into civil parishes. The colony was divided into military *posts* and districts: New Orleans, Natchitoches, Pointe Coupée, Opelousas, Attakapas, and the Illinois Country posts, among others
- **Population:** No FamilySearch population data was returned for this period; French colonial census rolls (*dénombrements*) were taken periodically (known enumerations include 1706, 1708, 1721, 1724, 1726, 1731, 1741, 1744, and 1766) and are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer
- **Religion:** Catholicism was the only legally recognized faith under French rule; the *Code Noir* (Louisiana edition, 1724) required the Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons and regulated their legal status
- **Languages:** French throughout the colonial period; notarial and church records are in French and require reading competency

## Boundary changes

- **1699–1762:** All of Louisiana under French sovereignty; records created at colonial posts and the Superior Council in New Orleans
- **1762 (Treaty of Fontainebleau):** West of the Mississippi (including New Orleans) ceded to Spain — but Spain did not take effective administrative control until 1769. Records from 1762–1769 remain in French but exist in a transitional administrative limbo
- **1763 (Treaty of Paris):** East of the Mississippi (including the Natchez district and Mobile) ceded to Britain and reorganized as British West Florida — researchers with ancestors in that region must look separately at British colonial records
- **Quirk:** Events from 1762–1769 fall under French documentation but Spanish legal authority. Search both French colonial and early Spanish colonial series when working this window; they overlap and are not cleanly separated

## Available record types

### Church records — **PRIMARY SOURCE FOR THIS PERIOD**
- **The Catholic Church was the sole legal record-keeper for vital events** (births/baptisms, marriages, burials) in French Louisiana. There was no civil vital registration
- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans:** registers survive from **1720**, making them the oldest continuous vital registers in what is now the United States ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- **Code Noir records:** Because the *Code Noir* required Catholic baptism of enslaved persons, church registers document both free colonists and enslaved individuals — a critical source for African-descended families in this period
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (Collection ID 1612905) — 987,654 records and 493,827 images; date range begins 1718, squarely within the French colonial era. Access: [familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
- **Language:** French; records require reading colonial French hands
- **Physical originals:** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans); diocesan archives at the Archdiocese of New Orleans

### Superior Council records (civil/judicial/administrative)
- The *Conseil Supérieur* produced Louisiana's nearest equivalent to civil records: land concessions (*concessions*), court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories, and succession records ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — partially digitized
- **Access:** Physical access with some online finding aids; not fully indexed online
- **Digitization level:** Partial — browse-only for most of the series; confirm current digitization status directly with the Louisiana Historical Center

### Notarial records (contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions)
- The New Orleans Notarial Archives hold records **from the 1730s onward** and constitute the oldest continuous notarial office in North America ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- Record types: contracts, wills, *actes de mariage* (marriage contracts), property transfers, manumissions
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, 1340 Poydras St., New Orleans — provides public access
- **Digitization level:** Physical/on-site; some series are being digitized but not fully available online
- **Language:** French

### Land records (concessions and grants)
- French land grants used the *concession* system — not the English metes-and-bounds or rectangular-survey systems
- Colonial land grants are documented in the **American State Papers: Public Lands** series and at the **Louisiana State Land Office** ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- **FamilySearch probate collection** (which may include estate and succession records): *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* (Collection ID 2078341) — 456,789 records, 228,394 images; date range begins 1756, covering the late French colonial period. Access: [familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)
- **BLM General Land Office (GLO):** [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) holds some colonial-era patent records that carried over after the Louisiana Purchase

### Colonial census rolls (*dénombrements*)
- No federal census exists for this period (the first U.S. federal census was 1790, after Louisiana joined the U.S. in 1803)
- French colonial censuses were taken periodically; they list household heads, family members, enslaved persons, livestock, and crops
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France — holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for the colony ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- **Digitization level:** ANOM has an online portal ([anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)) with partial digitization; census rolls are not fully indexed
- **Language:** French

### Military records
- Colonial military records document French regulars, colonial militia (*milice*), and post commandants
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) for French military series; some records in the Louisiana Historical Center
- **Digitization level:** Physical/on-site at ANOM; not widely available online
- **Note:** After 1769, Spanish military records replace French ones — check Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) for the transition period onward

### Immigration and passenger records
- French colonists arrived in waves, including transported indentured servants (*engagés*), soldiers, settlers, and enslaved Africans
- The *filles à la cassette* (Casket Girls) and other organized emigration schemes are partially documented in ANOM records and published genealogical studies
- **Where held:** ANOM for embarkation records; Louisiana Historical Center for local arrival records
- **Substitute:** Company of the Indies (*Compagnie des Indes*) records at ANOM document colonists brought under company auspices (1717–1731)

### Cemetery records
- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) has coverage for Louisiana, though colonial-era stone survival is limited due to climate and time
- Burial records from this period were kept by Catholic parishes — see Church Records above
- **Physical:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (New Orleans, est. 1789) is post-colonial; earlier burials were recorded in parish registers only

### Newspapers
- No newspapers were published in French Louisiana during the colonial period. The first Louisiana newspaper (*Le Moniteur de la Louisiane*) did not appear until 1794 — outside this target window

### Tax records
- Colonial tax/tribute records were kept at the post level and are held primarily at ANOM; some are in the Louisiana Historical Center
- These can substitute for missing census data for specific posts

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections relevant to French colonial Louisiana | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (1.6M imgs); *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* | Free |
| BLM General Land Office | Colonial-era land patents that survived into American records | Free |
| ANOM Online Portal | Partial digitization of colonial censuses, correspondence, military records | Free (partial) |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records, colonial-era archives, partially digitized | In-person / finding aids online |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s onward — contracts, wills, marriage settlements | In-person public access |
| Louisiana State Land Office (Baton Rouge) | Colonial land grant records, American State Papers | In-person / some online |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Census rolls, administrative correspondence, military records, Company of Indies records | In-person + partial online portal |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Records from the 1769–1803 Spanish period onward; relevant for the transition era | In-person + partial digitization |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Diocesan church records complementing parish registers | By appointment |

## Records NOT online (or only partially online)
- **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) records** — partially digitized at the Louisiana Historical Center; no complete online index
- **ANOM colonial censuses and correspondence** — partial digitization via ANOM portal; most require on-site or duplication requests
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives (1730s–1769)** — on-site access; not fully digitized
- **French colonial military records** — largely at ANOM, not widely indexed online
- **Post-level local records** from Natchitoches, Pointe Coupée, Opelousas, Attakapas — survival and access varies; some are at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge

## Known record losses and gaps
- **Pre-1720 church records:** No Catholic parish registers predate St. Louis Cathedral's 1720 series are known to survive in Louisiana repositories for the New Orleans area; earlier events must be sought in ANOM or published transcriptions
- **1788 and 1794 New Orleans fires:** Two major fires destroyed much of colonial-era New Orleans. Some Superior Council and notarial records were lost; however, notarial copies and ANOM duplicates partially compensate
- **British West Florida (1763–1781):** Records for the eastern (British-held) portion of Louisiana after 1763 are held in British colonial archives (The National Archives, Kew) and the Mississippi Department of Archives and History — not in Louisiana repositories

## Research tips

1. **Start with Catholic parish registers.** Church records are the single most important source for this period and the only vital record type that existed. FamilySearch's *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (collection 1612905) is your first stop online ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))

2. **The Code Noir created records for enslaved ancestors.** Because the law required Catholic baptism of all enslaved people, church registers name enslaved individuals — often with the enslaver's name as a reference point. This is frequently the only documentary trace of enslaved ancestors in the colonial period ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))

3. **Know which post your ancestor lived in.** Records were created at individual *posts* (New Orleans, Natchitoches, Pointe Coupée, etc.), not at a colony-wide level. Identify the post first, then target that post's church and administrative records

4. **ANOM is indispensable for this period.** French national archives (ANOM, Aix-en-Provence) hold material that never made it to Louisiana repositories — census rolls, emigration records, administrative correspondence naming colonists. Budget for an ANOM research request or hire a French-based genealogist if you cannot travel there

5. **Notarial records are an under-used treasure.** The New Orleans Notarial Archives (from the 1730s) record marriages, wills, manumissions, and contracts that are not captured elsewhere. These are particularly rich for free people of color and merchant families ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))

6. **Land concessions follow French law.** Colonial French grants are not searchable through the standard English-law deed search workflows. Work through the American State Papers: Public Lands series and the Louisiana State Land Office for grants that were confirmed after the Louisiana Purchase ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))

7. **Check ANOM's Company of Indies records (1717–1731).** The *Compagnie des Indes* controlled Louisiana colonization during that period and left separate passenger and personnel records from the broader French colonial administrative series

8. **Records in French require linguistic skill.** All colonial Louisiana records are in French, often in 18th-century hands. Plan for translation assistance or acquire reading skills before attempting original documents

9. **The 1762–1769 transition is a documentation seam.** Events in this window may appear in the tail end of French administrative series or in the opening of Spanish series. Search both; the Louisiana Historical Center and the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) together cover this overlap

10. **FamilySearch wiki tools returned generic content for Louisiana** — consult the Louisiana Genealogy page at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy) directly for the most current collection guidance

---

**Summary of top research priorities for French colonial Louisiana (1700–1769):**

| Priority | Record type | Where to search first | Digitization level |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | FamilySearch collection 1612905 | Indexed + images (from 1718) |
| 2 | Superior Council records (estates, contracts, land) | Louisiana Historical Center | Partial / browse-only |
| 3 | Notarial records (wills, marriage contracts) | New Orleans Notarial Archives | Physical / on-site |
| 4 | Colonial census rolls (*dénombrements*) | ANOM (France) online portal | Partial digital |
| 5 | Probate/estate records | FamilySearch collection 2078341 | Indexed + images (from 1756) |
| 6 | Military & emigration records | ANOM (France) | Physical / partial digital |

# Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Genealogy Research Guide (Late 1800s, c. 1860–1906)

---

## Jurisdictional Overview

Pennsylvania's coal mining communities divide into two regions, each with its own county structure:

**Anthracite (Hard Coal) — Northeastern PA:**
Schuylkill County (formed 1811; Pottsville, Shenandoah, Mahanoy City), Luzerne County (Wilkes-Barre, Hazleton, Plymouth), **Lackawanna County** (Scranton, Carbondale — **carved from Luzerne County on August 13, 1878**), Carbon County (Mauch Chunk / Jim Thorpe), and Northumberland County (Shamokin).

**Bituminous (Soft Coal) — Southwestern PA:**
Westmoreland, Fayette, Washington, Allegheny, Cambria (Johnstown), and Indiana counties.

**Critical boundary change:** Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878. All county-level records for the Scranton/Carbondale area before that date — deeds, marriages, naturalizations, probate — are filed under **Luzerne County**. Search Luzerne first for any event before August 1878, then Lackawanna after.

The region exploded demographically with successive immigration waves: Irish, Welsh, and German arrivals in the 1840s–1870s, followed by Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian miners from the 1880s onward. (Source: Wikipedia, *Coal Region*, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region)

---

## 1. Vital Records — ⚠ No Statewide Registration Until 1906

Pennsylvania **did not require statewide civil registration** of births and deaths until **1906**. Before that date, vital events for coal town families are recorded in:
- **Church registers** (primary source — see §2 below)
- **County-level registration** where it existed: Philadelphia from 1860; Allegheny from 1870
- **Family Bibles** and occasional newspaper notices

(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)

**Marriage records** were kept at the county level from the colonial period — marriage licenses and bonds at each county courthouse.

**FamilySearch indexed collections:**

| Collection | ID | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985 | [1401638](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638) | 1,245,830 | Indexed + images ✅ |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 312,045 | Indexed + images ✅ |
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 | [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 524,189 | Indexed + images ✅ |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 198,765 | Index only — no images ⚠ |
| Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 | [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) | 4,218,763 | Indexed + images ✅ |

Note: The death certificate collection begins in 1906, just after the late-1800s window — use it to capture early deaths of people whose lives began in your research period.

---

## 2. ⭐ Church Records — Highest Priority for Immigrant Mining Families

For the vast majority of coal town immigrants, **ethnic parish registers are the only pre-1906 vital records** that exist. They record baptisms (with birth date, parents' names, godparents, and often the village of origin in the old country), marriages, and burials.

Mining communities were organized tightly by ethnicity and denomination:

| Ethnic Group | Primary Denomination |
|---|---|
| Irish | Roman Catholic |
| Welsh | Congregational, Methodist, Baptist |
| German | Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic |
| Polish | Roman Catholic |
| Lithuanian | Roman Catholic |
| Slovak | Roman Catholic, Greek / Byzantine Catholic |
| Italian | Roman Catholic |
| Ukrainian | Greek / Byzantine (Ruthenian) Catholic |

(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)

**Key repositories:**
- **FamilySearch** — *Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985* (collection 1401638) is your first stop; it is 95%+ name-indexed.
- **Roman Catholic Diocese of Scranton** (anthracite) and the **Diocese of Pittsburgh / Diocese of Greensburg** (bituminous) — hold many registers not yet digitized; contact diocesan archives directly.
- Individual parishes — some records remain local; others have been transferred to diocesan archives or state historical societies.

---

## 3. Census Records

Federal decennial censuses covering the target period are available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com:

- **1860** — pre-boom baseline; occupation listed
- **1870** — captures the first large immigrant wave; lists birthplace
- **1880** — relationship to head of household added; Soundex index available
- **1900** — records parents' birthplaces and immigration year — crucial for immigrant families

**Mortality schedules** (1860, 1870, 1880) list everyone who died in the 12 months before the census with cause of death — an important source for identifying mine accident victims.

⚠ The **1890 federal census was largely destroyed** by fire in 1921. Substitute with 1880 + 1900, county tax records, and city directories.

**Search tip:** Look for occupation entries reading "miner," "coal miner," "laborer at mine," or "mine laborer" to identify target households. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)

External access: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/

---

## 4. ⛏ Coal Industry Records — Unique to This Region

### State Mine Inspector Reports (1870 onward)
Published annually from 1870, these are the most distinctive genealogical record class for the coal region. Each report lists **every fatal mine accident** that year with the victim's:
- Full name
- Age
- Nationality / country of origin
- Cause and date of death
- Mine name and location

**Held at:** Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg. (Sources: Wikipedia *Coal Region*; https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)

### Digitized Employment & Accident Volumes on FamilySearch

| Volume | DGS # | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill Mine Worker Employment Cards, 1870–1900 | 002240015 | 410 | **95% name-indexed + full-text searchable** ✅ |
| Luzerne Mine Accident Reports, 1870–1895 | 002240016 | 287 | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text ⚠ |
| Lackawanna Colliery Payroll Ledgers, 1878–1900 | 002240017 | 199 | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text ⚠ |

The Luzerne and Lackawanna volumes must be paged through image by image; there is no name search.

### Company Employment Records
Pay ledgers, accident reports, and employment cards survive **fragmentarily** at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties. Coverage is uneven — not every colliery's records survived.

### Union Records
The **United Mine Workers of America (UMWA)** was founded in 1890. Membership rolls and grievance files survive for many locals. Consult the UMWA archives and the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville).

---

## 5. Naturalization & Immigration Records

Nearly all late-1800s coal miners were immigrants or children of immigrants. Most entered through **Philadelphia** or **New York** (Ellis Island opened 1892; earlier arrivals used Castle Garden / Port of New York or the Port of Philadelphia).

**Pre-1906 naturalizations** could be filed in any court of record — Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, or Orphans' Court. After September 27, 1906, they were standardized and handled by the federal Bureau of Naturalization.

- **Schuylkill County naturalization records, 1840s–1906** — at the Pennsylvania State Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)
- Other coal counties' naturalization records — at respective county courthouses or microfilmed at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Post-1906 federal naturalization petitions** — at NARA: https://www.archives.gov/
- **Passenger lists** — on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com

---

## 6. Land, Tax & Probate Records

- **County deeds** begin at county formation; held at each county Recorder of Deeds; many are microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Probate records** (wills, estate inventories, guardianships, letters of administration) are at the county **Register of Wills** from county formation onward.
  - FamilySearch: *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* (collection [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) — 893,214 indexed records with images ✅
- **Tax assessment lists / tax duplicates** survive from the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties and are the best substitute for pre-1790 censuses; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and county historical societies.
- **Company store ledgers** — miners were often paid in company scrip redeemable only at the company store. Ledgers survive fragmentarily at local historical societies and can name every family's purchases year by year.

(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)

---

## 7. Military Records

- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Pennsylvania raised more than 360 regiments; many coal miners served. Service records and pension files are at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/). **Pension files** are particularly rich — they document the soldier's wife, children, marriage date, and birthplace.
- **Pennsylvania State Adjutant General records** — at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.

---

## 8. Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) has indexed many coal region cemeteries.
- Mining accidents sometimes resulted in mass burials at **ethnic parish cemeteries** (often the only known burial location for a victim).
- Many Welsh and Irish communities established their own denominational cemeteries in the 1850s–1880s, separate from Catholic parish grounds.

---

## 9. Newspapers

Historical newspapers are essential for mining accident reports, obituaries, and ethnic community columns (naming visitors, marriages, and deaths not recorded elsewhere).

- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) — the *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, Schuylkill County), published since 1825, is the most important coal region paper.
- The Pennsylvania State Library and local historical societies hold additional newspaper runs, including Welsh-language and Polish-language papers serving specific communities.

---

## 10. Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector reports (1870+); county naturalization records; tax lists; some company employment records |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Mining records, *Miners' Journal* files, local church records |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton, Lackawanna Co.) | Mining company records, ethnic community collections |
| **County Courthouse / Register of Wills** | Deeds, probate, marriage licenses — each county separately |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Census, church and town records, county marriages, probate, some mine employment volumes |
| **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal naturalization (post-1906), pension files, passenger lists |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, passenger lists |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service and pension records |
| **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery transcriptions |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspaper runs including the *Miners' Journal* |

---

## Key Quirks & Cautions

1. **No statewide birth/death registration until 1906.** Church registers are the primary vital record source for the late 1800s — identify your ancestor's ethnicity and denomination first. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)

2. **Lackawanna County formed from Luzerne County in 1878.** County records (deeds, marriages, naturalizations, probate) for the Scranton/Carbondale area before August 13, 1878 are under **Luzerne County** — search Luzerne first.

3. **The 1890 census is largely destroyed.** Bridge the gap with the 1880 and 1900 censuses, county tax assessment lists, and city directories.

4. **FamilySearch volumes DGS 002240016 (Luzerne Mine Accident Reports) and DGS 002240017 (Lackawanna Colliery Payroll Ledgers) are browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. You must page through them image by image with no search capability.

5. **Pre-1906 naturalizations can be in any court of record.** Check Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and Orphans' Court separately for each county where the ancestor lived.

6. **Ethnic parish identity is essential.** A Polish Catholic miner's baptismal record will be in the Polish national parish register, not the Irish parish across the street — even in the same town.

7. **Mine Inspector reports (1870+) are a unique finding aid** for fatal accident victims — they name individuals with ages and nationalities not available elsewhere.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States
## Early 1600s — Puritan Settlements (c. 1620–1700)

---

## Jurisdiction overview

**A critical distinction before anything else:** The early 1600s Massachusetts settlements were governed by **two entirely separate colonial jurisdictions** that must be researched independently:

- **Plymouth Colony (1620–1691):** Established by the Mayflower Separatists; governed Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol, and surrounding areas. Its records are **published and indexed separately** from those of Massachusetts Bay Colony. ([Massachusetts Church Records – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691):** The dominant Puritan settlement governed by the General Court in Boston. Governor John Winthrop led the **Great Migration** of approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640. (*Wikipedia, Massachusetts Bay Colony*)

In **1691**, both colonies merged into the **Province of Massachusetts Bay** under a royal charter.

**County structure:** Massachusetts Bay Colony created its first four counties in **1643** — Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, and old Norfolk (which then encompassed towns now in New Hampshire and Maine). **Before 1643, no county structure existed** — all records were maintained at the **town** and **General Court** levels only.

**Religious denominations:** Congregationalism was the established church; no other denomination held official recognition. Quakers were actively persecuted (four executed, 1659–1661). Small numbers of Anglicans and Baptists were present from the 1630s onward.

**Key event affecting records:** King Philip's War (1675–1676) — the most destructive conflict of the period — disrupted many communities and may have caused localized record gaps.

---

## Boundary changes

| Period | Situation |
|--------|-----------|
| 1620–1643 | No county structure; all records held at town and General Court level |
| 1643 | Four original counties created: Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, old Norfolk |
| 1643–1700 | Additional counties carved from originals — researcher must know the correct county *at the time of the event*, not today's boundaries |
| 1620–1691 | Plymouth Colony is a **fully separate jurisdiction** — court records, land records, and vital registers are entirely distinct |
| 1691 | Province of Massachusetts Bay unites both colonies under one royal charter |

> **Quirk:** Old Norfolk County (1643) included towns now in New Hampshire. Records for those towns before New Hampshire became a separate province may appear in Massachusetts Bay Colony court records rather than in any NH repository.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil/town registration)

- **Town-level recording mandated from 1639:** The Massachusetts Bay General Court ordered towns to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** — one of the earliest civil registration mandates in North America. This is a **town-level** requirement; statewide registration did not begin until **1841** and is irrelevant to the 1600s entirely. ([Massachusetts Genealogy – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **FamilySearch — indexed + images:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (collection [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550); 3,456,789 records; 1,728,394 images) — overlaps the full target period.
- **Published abstracts:** The **Tanner–Corbin "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is a standard starting point. Available at NEHGS, university libraries, and digitally via Internet Archive. ([Massachusetts Genealogy – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Plymouth Colony:** Vital registration was kept separately under Plymouth Colony's own system; records are published and indexed independently. ([Massachusetts Church Records – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Gap warning:** Individual town compliance with the 1639 mandate varied. A missing entry does not mean the event did not occur — always cross-check church records.

### Church records

- **Most important record type for the earliest decades.** Congregational church records are the single most critical genealogical source for pre-1650 Massachusetts, when town recording was still inconsistent. ([Massachusetts Church Records – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications and admonishments). (*Wikipedia, Massachusetts Bay Colony*)
- **FamilySearch — indexed + images:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (collection [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657); 987,654 records; 493,827 images) — starts in the target period.
- **Published sources:** Many early Congregational registers have been published in the **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** series and in local historical society publications. ([Massachusetts Church Records – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Physical repositories:** Original registers remain with individual congregations or have been deposited at the Massachusetts Archives, NEHGS, or local historical societies — the FamilySearch collection is partial.

### Census records

- **No federal census before 1790** — entirely outside the 1600s target period.
- **No formal colonial census** existed in Massachusetts during this period.
- **Substitutes:** Town rate/tax lists, militia musters, and freeman lists served enumeration functions. Some survive in town records and Massachusetts Archives collections — see Tax Records below.

### Probate and court records

- **FamilySearch — indexed + images:** *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* (collection [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901); 567,890 records; 283,945 images) — begins squarely in the target period.
- **Before 1643:** The colony's General Court served as the probate authority; records are in Massachusetts Archives colony-court holdings.
- **After 1643:** County probate courts assumed jurisdiction. ([Massachusetts Church Records – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Plymouth Colony:** Separate court and probate records, published in Nathaniel Shurtleff's *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (in print; available at NEHGS and Internet Archive).
- **Research value:** Probate inventories name heirs, reveal family relationships, and list personal property — invaluable when vital records are thin.

### Land records

- **System:** Metes-and-bounds (state-land state; no federal land office). **Town proprietors' records** are a distinct and critically important source for the earliest period (1620s–1650s), documenting original land divisions before the county deed-recording system was established.
- **County deeds from the 1630s:** Deeds were recorded at county registries of deeds from as early as the 1630s, in remarkably complete runs. ([Massachusetts Church Records – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Online availability:** No separate 1600s land collection appeared in the FamilySearch collections search; access is primarily through county registries and NEHGS. Some counties have digitized deed books online; others require in-person access.
- **Physical repositories:** Individual county registries of deeds; Massachusetts Archives for colony-era land grants.

### Military records

| Conflict | Dates | Record types | Where held |
|----------|-------|-------------|-----------|
| Pequot War | 1636–1638 | Militia muster rolls, General Court records | Massachusetts Archives |
| King Philip's War | 1675–1676 | Muster rolls, service lists, Court petitions | Massachusetts Archives; some published |

- **No federal military records** exist for this period — the U.S. military record system postdates independence. The Fold3 link returned as an external resource applies only to post-1775 records.

### Cemetery records

- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) — returned as a FamilySearch-curated external resource; covers many early Massachusetts burial grounds, including colonial-era town cemeteries.
- **Headstone transcriptions:** Many early colonial graveyards have been transcribed by the DAR and local genealogical societies; published volumes available at NEHGS.
- **Sexton records:** Sparse for the 1600s; headstone inscriptions are typically the primary burial source.

### Newspaper records

> ⚠️ **Not applicable for this target period.** The first Massachusetts newspaper (*Publick Occurrences*) appeared briefly in 1690; regular publication did not begin until *The Boston News-Letter* in 1704. **Newspapers.com**, returned as an external resource, is not relevant for 1600s research. Legal notices and community events from this era appear instead in General Court records and town meeting minutes.

### Immigration — the Great Migration

- **The Great Migration (1630–1643):** ~20,000 Puritan settlers arrived in Massachusetts; this is the primary immigration event of the target period. (*Wikipedia, Massachusetts Bay Colony*)
- **NEHGS Great Migration Study:** Documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643, with detailed genealogical profiles compiled from all available sources — the **essential starting point** for any 17th-century Massachusetts family. ([Massachusetts Genealogy – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **FamilySearch Passenger Lists** (collection 1784312, 1820–1891): **Does not cover the 1600s.** Out of period; do not use for this research.
- **17th-century ship lists:** Scattered across published genealogical compilations (e.g., Charles Banks, *The Planters of the Commonwealth*, 1930; available at NEHGS and Internet Archive). No single online database covers them comprehensively.

### Tax records

- **Town rate lists** (property taxes assessed by town selectmen) survive in many town archives from the 1640s onward.
- **Best census substitute** for this period — they can confirm presence in a town across years when no vital record exists.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices, Massachusetts Archives, and local historical societies. Digitization is uneven; many remain physical only.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (3.4M records); Church Records 1630–1920 (987K records); Probate Records 1635–1991 (567K records) | Free |
| **NEHGS – AmericanAncestors.org** | Great Migration Study; manuscript collections; published genealogies; Tanner–Corbin series | Subscription / member |
| **Internet Archive** | Tanner–Corbin vital records abstracts; 17th-century ship lists; Colonial Society of Massachusetts publications | Free |
| **FindAGrave** | Colonial-era cemetery records statewide | Free |
| **Fold3 / NARA** | *Post-1775 federal records only — not applicable for 1600s* | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | *No Massachusetts newspapers in the 1600s — not applicable* | Subscription |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | Colony court records from 1620s; governor's correspondence; General Court records; colonial militia records | In-person / online catalog |
| **NEHGS, Boston** | Great Migration Study; manuscripts; Tanner–Corbin series; published genealogies | In-person (free) / online subscription |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Deed books from the 1630s (per county) | In-person; availability varies by county |
| **County Probate Courts** | Probate files from 1643 (earlier in General Court records) | In-person; partially at FamilySearch |
| **Town Clerk Offices** | Original town vital records and meeting minutes | In-person; abstracted in Tanner–Corbin series |
| **Local Historical Societies** | Town histories, family genealogies, gravestone transcriptions | In-person; hours vary |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Original town meeting minutes and rate/tax lists** — largely physical only; digitization is uneven beyond the FamilySearch Town Vital Records collection.
- **County deed books** — county registries of deeds; online access varies widely by county and time period.
- **Colonial General Court and county court records** — Massachusetts Archives; some transcribed/published in print but not comprehensively digitized.
- **Many Congregational church registers** — originals with local congregations or deposited at NEHGS; the FamilySearch church records collection is partial coverage only.
- **Plymouth Colony records** — published in print (Shurtleff's *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth*; Plymouth Court Records); not fully digitized online.
- **17th-century ship passenger lists** — no comprehensive online database; found only in scattered published genealogical compilations.
- **Proprietors' records** — original town land-division books; many published by local historical societies but not in a single online repository.

---

## Known record losses

- Tool results did not surface documentation of specific courthouse fires or systematic record destructions for this period.
- **King Philip's War (1675–1676)** caused significant community disruption; localized record gaps are likely for towns in the conflict zone, but the full extent is not confirmed in the survey data.
- **Uneven compliance** with the 1639 vital-records mandate: some towns recorded diligently from the start; others did not. Treat a missing entry as a research gap, not proof of non-occurrence.

---

## Research tips

1. **Distinguish Plymouth Colony from Massachusetts Bay Colony** before searching anything. Confirm which colonial jurisdiction your ancestor's town belonged to before 1691 — records, courts, and published indexes are entirely separate. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))

2. **Town-level vital recording began in 1639 — not 1841.** The 1841 date applies only to *statewide* registration and is irrelevant here. Search the town clerk record first, then the Tanner–Corbin abstracts for that town. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

3. **Start with the NEHGS Great Migration Study** for any ancestor arriving before 1643 — it is the single most comprehensive compiled resource for early Massachusetts families, drawing on all known sources. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

4. **Know your county formation dates.** Before 1643, there are no county records — go directly to Massachusetts Archives General Court records. After 1643, determine the correct county for the town *at the date of the event*, since new counties were carved out across the period.

5. **Congregational church records often predate and supplement town vital records**, especially for the 1620s–1650s. Treat church registers as a co-equal primary source, not a backup.

6. **Proprietors' records are the land source for the 1620s–1640s**, before the county deed-recording system matured. Many have been published by local historical societies and are available at NEHGS.

7. **For King Philip's War ancestors (1675–1676):** Muster rolls and General Court petitions at the Massachusetts Archives may provide dates, locations, and family context unavailable elsewhere.

8. **The FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned only generic content** in this survey's tool calls — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy) for the most current, Massachusetts-specific guidance on collections and finding aids.

---
