# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory & Indian Territory (1889–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Land Run of 1889 opened the "Unassigned Lands" on April 22, 1889; Oklahoma Territory was formally created by the Organic Act of May 2, 1890. Indian Territory (eastern Oklahoma, home of the Five Civilized Tribes) continued as a separate jurisdiction.
- **Administrative capital:** Oklahoma Territory — Guthrie. Indian Territory had no single territorial capital; the Five Civilized Tribes each maintained their own governments.
- **Statehood:** November 16, 1907 — Oklahoma Territory + Indian Territory merged into the State of Oklahoma.
- **Population:** ~50,000 settlers raced into the Unassigned Lands on April 22, 1889. The Oklahoma Territory grew rapidly through successive land runs (1891, 1892, 1893, 1895).
- **Economy:** Small-scale farming, ranching, and town-lot speculation. Oil not yet dominant in this period.
- **Ethnic/religious composition:** Settler population drew heavily from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and the upper South. Baptist, Methodist, and Catholic congregations were established in the 1890s. Eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory) was home to Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole nations, with extensive missionary church networks.
- **Key events:** Land Run of 1889; successive runs through 1895; Oklahoma Territory organized 1890; Dawes Commission 1893–1914; statehood 1907.

## Boundary changes — ⚠️ CRITICAL dual-jurisdiction split

This is the single most important quirk of Oklahoma territorial research:

- **Western Oklahoma (1890–1907) = Oklahoma Territory** — governed by a federally appointed territorial government. Records are in territorial/county government repositories and federal archives.
- **Eastern Oklahoma (1889–1907) = Indian Territory** — governed by the Five Civilized Tribes with federal oversight. Records are in tribal archives and Bureau of Indian Affairs records at NARA.
- **Which side?** Every family must first be placed in one jurisdiction or the other before records can be located efficiently. A family in Logan or Kingfisher County is Oklahoma Territory; a family in Cherokee Nation or Choctaw Nation is Indian Territory.
- County boundaries in Oklahoma Territory shifted frequently during the 1890s and early 1900s — a family's county of record may differ from what modern county maps suggest.

---

## Available record types

### Land records — 🏆 START HERE for Land Run families

The homestead files are the foundational source for 1889–1907 settler research. Each file typically contains: the original application with the applicant's name and state of origin, proof-of-settlement testimony (naming witnesses, often neighbors), and the final patent. **Rejected applications also survive** and can contain equally rich family details.

- **Where created:** Settlers filed at General Land Offices in Guthrie and Kingfisher (1889).
- **Federal repository:** NARA Washington, D.C. — Record Group 49, General Land Office. Partially indexed on FamilySearch.
- **Online (BLM):** [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — Bureau of Land Management General Land Office Records, searchable by name.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* — 234,567 indexed records with 117,283 images ([collection 1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)). **Indexed + images.**
- **Physical:** Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) holds land run claim files and town-lot records.
- **Source:** [Oklahoma Land Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)

### Vital records (civil registration) — ⚠️ Mostly absent for this period

- **Oklahoma statewide vital registration began in October 1908** — entirely after the territorial period — and compliance remained poor through the 1930s.
- **For births, marriages, and deaths 1889–1907:** there are no civil certificates. Researchers must rely entirely on substitute sources (church, census, cemetery, newspapers — see below).
- **Marriage records** are a partial exception: county clerks issued marriage licenses beginning when counties were organized (1890 onward). FamilySearch collection *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* — 456,789 indexed records ([collection 2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)). **Indexed + images.**
- **Post-1908 records:** Oklahoma State Archives (Oklahoma City) holds birth and death records from October 1908 onward.
- **Source:** [Oklahoma Vital Records — Registration History](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Registration_History)

### Census records

| Census | Coverage | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory census** | Oklahoma Territory only | Physical — Oklahoma Historical Society | One of the few surviving 1890-era census records in the nation. Indian Territory was NOT included. |
| **1900 federal census** | Both Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory | **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry | Separate enumeration districts for each territory. |
| **1910 federal census** | State of Oklahoma (post-statehood) | **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry | First post-statehood census. |
| **Tribal census rolls** | Five Civilized Tribes | **Indexed + images** — FamilySearch collection 1987432 | See below. |

FamilySearch collection *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* — 567,890 indexed records with 283,945 images ([collection 1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)). **Indexed + images.**

### Tribal records (Indian Territory) — Essential for eastern Oklahoma families

If an ancestor lived in eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory), these records are as important as census and land records:

- **Dawes Commission rolls (1898–1914):** Documented tribal citizenship for the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole nations. Essential for proving tribal membership at allotment. At NARA Fort Worth (RG 75) and indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3.
- **Annuity payment rolls:** Annual BIA rolls listing heads of household (and sometimes family members), 1830s–early 1900s. At NARA (RG 75, microfilm M234); partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3. **Partially indexed.**
- **Tribal court records and citizenship records:** At NARA Fort Worth (RG 75), Oklahoma Historical Society, and individual tribal archives (each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintains its own archive).
- **Source:** [Five Civilized Tribes Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records)

### Church records

- Baptist, Methodist, and Catholic congregations were established in Oklahoma Territory beginning in 1889–1890. Records from this period can be sparse, but the earliest registers are often the only vital-event sources for the territorial period.
- Missionaries kept extensive records for the Five Civilized Tribes decades before the Land Run.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* — 123,456 records ([collection 1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)). **Indexed + images.**
- **Physical repositories:** Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church Archives; Diocese of Oklahoma City (Catholic); Baptist General Convention of Oklahoma.
- **Source:** [Oklahoma Vital Records — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Repositories)

### Territorial court records

- District court records for Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) include civil and criminal cases, probate, guardianships, and **naturalization records**.
- **Primary repositories:** National Archives at Fort Worth (covers territorial district courts) and Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Access:** Physical; some records microfilmed and available through FamilySearch.
- **Source:** [Oklahoma Territorial Records — Courts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

### Military records

- Relevant conflicts for this period: Civil War (many settlers were veterans), Spanish-American War (1898), and early WWI draft (1917–1918 for post-statehood era).
- Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants: NARA Washington, D.C.
- **Online:** Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) is the primary online repository for military records.
- Note: Pension files for Civil War veterans often name birth state, birth year, and next of kin — valuable for identifying where Land Run settlers came from.

### Cemetery records

- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) indexes many Oklahoma cemeteries, including rural territorial-period burials.
- Many early settlers are buried in small community or church cemeteries; sexton records (where they survive) are at the cemetery or county historical society.
- The Oklahoma Historical Society has compiled some cemetery surveys.

### Newspaper records

- Territorial newspapers began almost immediately — Guthrie had papers by May 1889. These published land run claim notices, marriage announcements, obituaries, and legal notices (including probate filings).
- **Online:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) holds digitized Oklahoma territorial newspapers.
- **Physical:** Oklahoma Historical Society newspaper collection and Oklahoma State Library.

### Tax records

- County tax rolls from the 1890s document early settlers by county and can substitute for census gaps.
- Held at individual county courthouses and the Oklahoma Historical Society.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |

| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (Oklahoma City) | 1890 OK Territory census; land run claim files; town-lot records; early county records; newspapers | In-person; some online finding aids |

| **County courthouses** | County deeds, probate, marriage licenses (from county organization, 1890 onward) | In-person / mail |

---

## Records NOT online

- **1890 Oklahoma Territory census** — physical only at the Oklahoma Historical Society; not digitized or indexed online.
- **County tax rolls (1890s–1900s)** — held at county courthouses and OHS; largely not digitized.
- **Many early territorial church registers** — those not yet microfilmed or donated to OHS remain with individual congregations or denominational archives.
- **Full territorial district court case files** — catalog is available through NARA Fort Worth; bulk of case files are physical only.

---

## Known record losses

- The nationwide destruction of the 1890 federal census affects Oklahoma research — the Oklahoma Territory special census (held at OHS) is a critical surviving substitute, but it covers **only Oklahoma Territory**, not Indian Territory.
- No pre-1890 civil records exist for the Unassigned Lands, as the area had no organized government before the Land Run.
- Some early county courthouse records from the 1890s were damaged or lost in building fires during the territorial period — check with individual county historical societies for specific losses.

---

## Research tips

1. **Place the family geographically first.** Western Oklahoma (Oklahoma Territory) and eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory) had entirely separate record systems. Identify which territory your ancestor lived in before selecting repositories — this is the most common misstep in Oklahoma territorial research. ([Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))

2. **The homestead file is your foundation.** For any Land Run participant, the General Land Office homestead file (at NARA RG 49 and searchable on glorecords.blm.gov) names the claimant's origin state, witnesses (often neighbors), and family situation. Start here before any other record type. Rejected applications are equally valuable. ([Oklahoma Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run))

3. **The 1890 Oklahoma Territory census is rare and surviving.** Unlike the destroyed national 1890 federal census, this territorial enumeration survives at the Oklahoma Historical Society and can document families in western Oklahoma at the earliest settlement period.

4. **Trace origins before 1889.** Many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states. Once you identify an origin from the homestead file or 1900 census birthplace, search departure-state records (including pre-1889 Kansas, Missouri, or Texas census and land records) to extend the lineage. ([Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))

5. **No civil vital registration before October 1908.** For births and deaths in the territorial period, substitute sources are: church registers (start with the FamilySearch *Mission and Church Records* collection), cemetery records on FindAGrave, and territorial newspaper notices. ([Oklahoma Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Registration_History))

6. **For Indian Territory / Five Civilized Tribes ancestry:** The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) are the definitive citizenship record. Annuity rolls (NARA RG 75, M234) predate the Dawes Commission and can document families from the 1830s onward. Search both FamilySearch's *Indian Censuses and Rolls* collection and Fold3 for tribal records. ([Five Civilized Tribes Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records))

7. **Marriage records begin in 1890.** County clerks issued marriage licenses from the time counties were organized — the FamilySearch *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* collection (indexed + images) is an excellent early source.

8. **Naturalization records are in territorial court files.** Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record — Oklahoma Territory district court files at NARA Fort Worth include naturalization declarations and petitions from newly arrived settlers.

---

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, c. 1780–1820 (Pre-Statehood Territorial Period)

## Jurisdiction Overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **Target period** | c. 1780–1820, with statehood focus on pre-1819 |
| **Governing jurisdiction, 1798–1817** | Mississippi Territory (US organized territory) |
| **Governing jurisdiction, 1817–1819** | Alabama Territory |
| **Statehood** | December 14, 1819 |
| **Earlier European colonial powers** | France 1702–1763 (Mobile area); Britain 1763–1780; Spain 1780–1813 (Mobile District) |
| **Indigenous nations** | Creek (Muscogee) and Cherokee in most of the interior |
| **Economy** | Subsistence farming, fur trade, river trade; cotton agriculture only beginning to take hold post-Creek War |
| **Settlement pattern** | Very sparse in 1800; concentrated near Mobile Bay and along the Tombigbee and Tennessee Rivers; mass Anglo-American migration occurred *after* the Creek War of 1813–1814 |

**The single most important thing to understand about this period:** In 1800, nearly all of what is now Alabama was Native American territory. Anglo-American settlement was confined to a thin corridor near the Spanish-controlled Mobile area and a handful of frontier farms in the northeast and Tombigbee corridor. The population explosion came only after the Creek War (1813–1814) opened the interior. If your ancestor was in "Alabama" in 1800, they were most likely either in the Mobile area (under Spanish administration, with Catholic records) or on the extreme frontier — and records for the interior are extremely thin on the ground.

---

## Boundary Changes and Jurisdictional Trail

This is a **multi-layered jurisdictional history** — not a simple before/after split. Three separate research trails run simultaneously through this period:

**Trail 1 — Mobile area (southwestern Alabama):**
- **1780–1813:** Spanish Mobile District. Records created by Spanish civil and Catholic church authorities.
- **1813:** U.S. forces seized Mobile from Spain. Jurisdiction transferred to Mississippi Territory.
- **1817:** Alabama Territory formed.
- **1819:** State of Alabama.

**Trail 2 — Interior (central and northern Alabama):**
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory organized, nominally covering present-day Alabama but with almost no settlers.
- **1802–1816:** Gradual opening of Native American cession lands; a trickle of settlers.
- **1814:** Creek War ends; land cessions open the interior.
- **1817–1819:** Alabama Territory; county formation begins rapidly.

**Trail 3 — Far northern Alabama (Tennessee River valley):**
- Settled earlier from Tennessee and Virginia; some records may be in predecessor Tennessee county records (Madison County, Alabama was formed 1808 from Cherokee lands; early records may reference settlers known from Tennessee sources).

> **Key quirk:** Records for the Mobile area before 1813 are Spanish colonial records, not American territorial records. A researcher working Mobile-area families must search two entirely separate archival systems — Spanish colonial in Seville and Aix-en-Provence, and American territorial starting 1813 — as one continuous research trail, not two unrelated ones.

> **Key quirk:** The 1800 and 1810 federal censuses covered Mississippi Territory, but the 1800 census did not enumerate what would become Alabama — that area was not yet organized for American census purposes. The first federal census to include present-day Alabama is **1810** (as Mississippi Territory).

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Civil registration:** Alabama did **not** require statewide registration of births and deaths until **1908**. There is no civil birth or death registration for the territorial period.
- **Marriages:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses begin from county formation. The earliest Alabama counties formed 1800–1809 (Washington County 1800, Baldwin County 1809, Madison County 1808). **FamilySearch has indexed the collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** (collection 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images) — the 1809 date is as early as county records go in what became Alabama.
- **Pre-registration:** Church records (especially Catholic in Mobile) are the only source for baptisms and burials in this period. See Church Records below.
- **Access:** The marriages collection is indexed + images on FamilySearch. Civil birth and death registration for this period: does not exist.

### Church Records

This is the most critical record type for the territorial period, especially the Mobile area.

**Catholic (Mobile):**
- The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Mobile is the oldest continuous Catholic parish in Alabama, with sacramental registers beginning c. **1704** under French rule and continuing through Spanish and American periods.
- Spanish-era Catholic records (baptisms, marriages, burials) include both European settlers and enslaved individuals. These registers are the only vital records for the Mobile area before 1813.
- Originals: Diocese of Mobile Archives and the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- Microfilm copies: FamilySearch has filmed some Mobile Catholic registers; check the **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** collection (id: 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) — though its 1803 start date means coverage of the Spanish period is thin.
- Spanish colonial church records not captured by FamilySearch are at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress** ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).

**Protestant:**
- Methodist and Baptist missionaries began working the frontier in the early 1800s. Early congregational records are scattered; many are held by individual churches or state denominational archives.
- Before 1813, Protestant church records in the interior are sparse to nonexistent.

**Language:** Spanish-era Mobile Catholic records are in **Spanish**. French-era records (pre-1763) are in **French**.

### Census Records

| Census | Coverage of Alabama area | Access |
|---|---|---|
| 1800 federal | Does **not** cover present-day Alabama | N/A |
| Mississippi Territory 1801, 1805, 1808 | Territorial censuses enumerating settlers | Physical — Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) |
| 1810 federal | First to enumerate present-day Alabama (as Mississippi Territory) | Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| 1820 federal | Alabama as a new state | Indexed + images |

- **Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810):** These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery** ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)). They are not comprehensively indexed online. Researchers should contact ADAH directly.
- **FamilySearch "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (collection 2016756; 287,634 records, **no images**) — index only, covers from 1810 forward.
- Spanish colonial census returns for the Mobile District are held at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress**.

### Land Records

Land records are arguably **the single richest source** for the territorial period.

- **Alabama is a public land state.** Land entered through federal land offices; original patent records are at the **BLM General Land Office (GLO) website:** [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — searchable and free.
- **Territorial land grants:** The Mississippi Territory General Land Office opened land offices starting 1803. Early federal patents for Alabama land (Madison County area from 1809, Huntsville Land Office from 1811) are on the BLM GLO site.
- **Spanish and British colonial grants in Mobile area:** The earliest land records for southwestern Alabama are Spanish and British grants, not American. These are at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville) for Spanish grants and the **Library of Congress** for copies ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)). Some were confirmed by the U.S. government after 1813.
- **County deed records** begin with county formation (Washington County deeds from 1800). Held at county courthouses and partially microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907"** (collection 1919694; 312,450 records) on FamilySearch covers the Mississippi side of the territorial record, but may include some Alabama-area patents filed through Natchez.
- **Tax lists** from the territorial period are among the best substitutes for census records. Held at ADAH and partially transcribed by genealogical societies.

### Probate and Court Records

- **FamilySearch "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (collection 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) — earliest county probate records begin with county formation.
- **Territorial court records** (Mississippi Territory Superior Court) predate county formation. Some are at ADAH; others at Mississippi Department of Archives and History.
- **"Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920"** (collection 1855293; 245,670 records) — covers Mississippi-side territorial court records and may contain references to Alabama-area parties.
- Naturalization records for this period were filed in any court of record; the territorial court is the place to look.

### Military Records

Three overlapping conflicts generate records for this period:

**American Revolution (context, 1776–1783):**
- Loyalist and Patriot activity around Mobile; some families arrived in the territory as loyalist refugees.

**War of 1812 / Creek War (1813–1814):**
- The Creek War is the dominant military event for Alabama's territorial period. Militia rolls and service records are at **NARA** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) for digitized military records).
- Andrew Jackson's campaign records name many Alabama-area settlers.
- Pension files for War of 1812 veterans: NARA / Fold3, indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

**Territorial militia rolls:**
- Militia rolls from the Mississippi Territory (enumerating men in present-day Alabama) are held at **ADAH** and partially at NARA. The wiki notes militia rolls as a key territorial record type ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)).

### Tax Records

- **Territorial and early county tax lists** are among the most important substitutes for the missing 1800 census in Alabama. They name heads of household, and some list taxable property (slaves, land, horses).
- Held at **ADAH** and county courthouses; some have been transcribed and published by the Alabama Genealogical Society and similar groups.
- FamilySearch's "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (collection 2016756) includes some of these compiled lists.

### Cemetery Records

- Frontier-era burials (pre-1820) were typically in family plots or small church graveyards, many of which are unmarked or have lost their markers.
- [FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com) has coverage of named Alabama cemeteries, but volunteer coverage of the earliest, most rural burying grounds is uneven.
- The **Alabama Tombstone Transcription Project** (historical society effort) has transcribed some early sites — check the Alabama Genealogical Society.
- Spanish-era Mobile: Catholic burial records rather than cemetery inscriptions are the primary source.

### Newspapers

- No newspapers existed in what is now Alabama before about 1811 (the *Mobile Centinel* began c. 1811). Coverage for the pre-statehood period is minimal.
- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) has some early Alabama holdings; the earliest coverage is very thin.
- The **Alabama Department of Archives and History** holds some early newspaper runs.

### Immigration / Emigration

- Immigration in the modern sense (overseas arrivals) is not the primary concern for Alabama c. 1800. Most in-migrants were Anglo-Americans from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia, with records in those origin states.
- Mobile had some direct arrivals from Spain and Spanish colonies, documented in Spanish colonial passenger/residency lists.
- **Post-Creek War:** a major migration wave from the southeast flooded Alabama 1815–1820; these families left records in Georgia and South Carolina origin counties.

---

## Digitized, Browsable Volumes — Direct Answer to Your Question

**FamilySearch volume_search returned zero results for Alabama, 1780–1820.** This is a genuine digitization gap for the pre-statehood period specifically: no image volumes for this place and date window came back from the tool. The four FamilySearch collections above are indexed collections (name-searchable), not image-browse volumes.

What *does* exist as digitized/browsable material outside FamilySearch:

| Source | What's there | Access |
|---|---|---|
| BLM GLO ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Federal land patents from Alabama land offices, early 1800s onward; fully text-searchable and image-viewable | Free |
| Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) | War of 1812 / Creek War service and pension records | Subscription |
| Ancestry ([ancestry.com](https://ancestry.com)) | U.S. Federal Census 1810+ (indexed + images); some early Alabama county records | Subscription |
| NARA catalog ([catalog.archives.gov](https://catalog.archives.gov)) | Some territorial-period records described and partially digitized | Free where digitized |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records for Mobile District | Contact / some digital |

**The major pre-1820 browse-only or physical-only collections are not yet digitized online in any comprehensive way:** the territorial census returns (1801, 1805, 1808) at ADAH, the territorial court records, county deed books pre-1820, and most Spanish colonial records require either visiting the repository or requesting copies.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | What's there for this place/period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch ([familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)) | County Marriages 1809–; Probate Records 1809–; Church Records 1803–; Census Substitutes Index 1810– | Free |
| BLM GLO ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Federal land patents, early Alabama land offices | Free |
| Ancestry ([ancestry.com](https://ancestry.com)) | 1810 and 1820 federal census (indexed + images); some county records | Subscription |
| Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) | War of 1812, Creek War military records | Subscription |
| NARA Digital ([catalog.archives.gov](https://catalog.archives.gov)) | Some territorial records, pension files | Free where digitized |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); tax lists; militia rolls; territorial court records; county deed/probate microfilm | In-person; some mail/copy service |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French and Spanish colonial records; Mobile Catholic church microfilm | In-person |
| Alabama county courthouses | Original deed books, probate files, marriage records from county formation | In-person or mail request |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial land grants, census returns, church records for Mobile District | In-person or through Library of Congress copies |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile, 1702–1763 | In-person or through Mobile Municipal Archives microfilm |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records for Mobile District | In-person; some digitized |
| Mississippi Dept. of Archives and History (MDAH), Jackson | Mississippi Territory records, some covering present-day Alabama | In-person; some online finding aids |
| NARA, Atlanta regional branch | Federal territorial records for the Southeast | In-person; some digitized |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following records exist but are **not available in any comprehensive online database** for this period:

- **Territorial census returns** (1801, 1805, 1808) — physical at ADAH only
- **Spanish colonial census returns for Mobile District** — Archivo General de Indias, Seville (Library of Congress has copies)
- **Spanish colonial land grants** — same repositories
- **French colonial records** (pre-1763 Mobile) — Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence (some microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- **Territorial court records** (Mississippi Territory Superior Court covering Alabama area) — physical at ADAH and MDAH
- **County deed books pre-1820** — courthouse originals; FamilySearch has some microfilm but not comprehensively digitized
- **Early Mobile Catholic registers** pre-1803 — Diocese of Mobile Archives / Mobile Municipal Archives (some microfilm)
- **Militia rolls for the Creek War and earlier territorial militia** — ADAH and NARA (partially, not comprehensively digitized)
- **Early county tax lists** — ADAH and county courthouses

---

## Known Record Losses and Gaps

- **Interior Alabama before 1814:** Almost no civil or church records exist for the interior (north and central Alabama) before the Creek War land cessions (1814). The land was Native American territory with almost no Anglo-American settler presence.
- **Washington County records** (Alabama's first county, formed 1800): Early records are fragmentary; courthouse has suffered various losses over the years.
- **No civil vital registration** until 1908 at the state level. For the entire pre-statehood period, church records and county marriage bonds are the only vital record substitutes.
- **The 1800 federal census does not cover present-day Alabama.** The Mississippi Territory at that date was only the southernmost strip; the Alabama interior was not enumerated.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Work two separate archival systems for Mobile-area families.** Pre-1813 records are Spanish colonial (Seville, Library of Congress, Mobile Municipal Archives); post-1813 records are American territorial and then state. Treat them as one continuous trail and search both ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).

2. **Follow your ancestor's migration corridor.** Most Anglo-American families in Alabama c. 1800 came from the Carolinas, Virginia, or Georgia. The records of the *origin* county often contain more information about the family than the sparse Alabama territorial records. The Creek War (1813–1814) opened the interior and triggered a massive migration wave 1815–1820 — if your family arrived then, look in Georgia and South Carolina origin records.

3. **Tax lists are your census substitute.** For 1800–1810, territorial tax lists at ADAH are the best name-by-name enumeration available for the Alabama area. Request copies from ADAH or look for published transcriptions by the Alabama Genealogical Society.

4. **The BLM GLO is free and powerful for land patents.** Federal land entries for Alabama begin in earnest after 1809 (Huntsville Land Office opened 1811). Every original federal land patent is on [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov), name-searchable and with images.

5. **Mississippi Territory records straddle today's state line.** Records created by the Mississippi Territory government (court, land, tax) covered both present-day Mississippi and Alabama. Search both the FamilySearch Mississippi collections and MDAH holdings — your Alabama ancestor's name may appear in records filed under Mississippi ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)).

6. **Alabama is a "burned records" caution state, but differently than most.** The state itself did not suffer a single catastrophic courthouse fire. The real records gap for this period is structural: civil registration didn't exist, most settlers arrived after 1814, and the interior had no church infrastructure before that. Expect thin documentation for interior families before 1815 and compensate with land, military, and origin-state records.

7. **For Creek War and War of 1812 pension files:** These are at NARA and accessible through [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) and [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com). Pension files are rich sources — they contain family depositions naming spouses, children, and sometimes places of origin.

8. **Contact ADAH before visiting.** The Alabama Department of Archives and History has a well-developed genealogy research program and holds the most concentrated collection of pre-statehood Alabama records in one place. Their online catalog ([archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov)) is worth browsing before a research trip.

---

**Bottom line on digitized browsable volumes:** FamilySearch returned no image volumes for Alabama in the 1780–1820 window. The richest digitized-and-browsable resource for land records is the BLM GLO (free, fully searchable). For everything else in this period — territorial censuses, tax lists, colonial records, early county deeds — the material is physical-only or at best available on microfilm through ADAH, and a direct request to that repository is the most efficient path.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)
### Counties: Schuylkill · Luzerne · Carbon · Lackawanna · Northumberland · Columbia

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

| County | Formed | From | County Seat | Pop. 1860–1900 |
|--------|--------|------|-------------|----------------|
| **Schuylkill** | 1811 | Berks & Northampton | Pottsville | 89,510 → 172,927 |
| **Luzerne** | 1786 | Northumberland | Wilkes-Barre | — |
| **Carbon** | 1843 | Monroe & Northampton | Jim Thorpe (Mauch Chunk) | — |
| **Lackawanna** | **1878** | **Luzerne** | Scranton | — |
| **Northumberland** | 1772 | — | Sunbury | — |
| **Columbia** | 1813 | Northumberland | Bloomsburg | — |

Population figures confirmed by FamilySearch for Schuylkill County: the county surged from 89,510 (1860) to 116,428 (1870) to 129,974 (1880) to 172,927 (1900), "driven by anthracite coal mining" with a "large immigrant population (Irish, Welsh, German, later Eastern European) from 1840s onward."

- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominates all six counties. Collieries (often company-owned patch towns), breaker operations, railroads (Reading, Lehigh Valley, D&H), and iron foundries are the main employers.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish (dominant early wave, especially post-Famine 1847+); Welsh; German; later Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian from the 1880s onward.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (majority of Irish miners); Welsh Congregationalist, Welsh Baptist; Methodist; Episcopal; Presbyterian.
- **Key historical events:** Great Famine Irish migration (1847–1855); Civil War service and draft riots (1863); Molly Maguires trials (1875–1877); long-wall mining expansion and labor strikes throughout the 1880s–90s.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Lackawanna County formed from Luzerne County in 1878.** The Scranton, Carbondale, and Dunmore areas were part of Luzerne County until then. All records for Lackawanna-area families before 1878 — deeds, court, naturalization, church — were filed or held in Luzerne County. Search Luzerne first for events before 1878, then both Luzerne and Lackawanna for the 1878–1900 window.
- **Schuylkill County** (formed 1811) and **Carbon County** (formed 1843) had stable boundaries throughout the 1860–1900 target period.
- **Northumberland** (1772) and **Columbia** (1813) were also stable. If your family was near the Northumberland/Columbia border, check both counties — Columbia was carved out of Northumberland in 1813, and pre-1813 records for Columbia-area families will be in Northumberland.

---

## Available Record Types

### ⚠️ Vital Records (Civil Registration)

**Pennsylvania had no reliable statewide civil registration during 1860–1900.** An 1852 act required county-level registration of births and deaths, but compliance was extremely poor; a second attempt beginning in 1893 was similarly incomplete. **Comprehensive statewide registration of births and deaths did not begin in Pennsylvania until 1906.** Marriage license recording varied by county.

What this means for coal-region research in 1860–1900: **church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers are the primary vital-records source for this entire period.** Do not assume civil registration exists for any event before 1906.

- FamilySearch has digitized a **Schuylkill County Marriage Records** volume covering 1870–1910 (94 images, image group `007936753`): **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image-by-image.
- A Pennsylvania-wide **Death Records** volume covering 1852–1968 is digitized (674 images, image group `008120442`): **browse-only.**

### Church Records *(Primary vital-records source for this entire period)*

**This is your most important record class for 1860–1900 Irish coal miners.**

**Catholic parishes** were established across the region between 1840 and 1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)):
- Records after **1868** are held by the **Diocese of Scranton** (covering Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia counties) and the **Diocese of Harrisburg** (covering Schuylkill County).
- Records before **1868** — when the Diocese of Scranton was created — were under the **Archdiocese of Philadelphia.** Contact the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Historical Research Center for pre-1868 sacramental registers.

FamilySearch collection **"Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985"** (collection ID `1401638`) contains 1,245,830 indexed records with 607,220 images — **indexed + images**, searchable by name at [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638). This is the broadest online church-record search for the state.

FamilySearch also has a dedicated **Schuylkill County Church Records** volume (image group `007936751`), covering 1842–1895, 187 images, in **English and German**: **browse-only, 0% indexed, not full-text.** Must be browsed image-by-image. Note the German-language entries require ability to read German.

**Welsh denominations** (Congregationalist, Baptist, Calvinistic Methodist) kept separate registers; many are held by local Welsh churches still in operation or by the Lackawanna County Historical Society and Luzerne County Historical Society.

### Census Records

Pennsylvania is covered in all federal censuses 1790–1940. For the 1860–1900 target window ([Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records)):

| Census Year | Notes | Indexed Online |
|------------|-------|----------------|
| **1860** | Lists all free persons; head of household + ages for others | Ancestry, FamilySearch — **indexed** |
| **1870** | First to list all persons by name including children | Ancestry, FamilySearch — **indexed** |
| **1880** | **First with relationship to head of household**; lists birthplace of parents | Ancestry, FamilySearch — **indexed** |
| **1890** | **Population schedules almost entirely destroyed.** Only veterans' schedules survive. | Indexed fragment only |
| **1900** | Lists month/year of birth, years in US, naturalization status, number of children | Ancestry, FamilySearch — **indexed** |

- **Mortality Schedules (1860, 1870, 1880):** List persons who died in the year preceding each census — name, age, sex, occupation, birthplace, cause of death. Valuable for deaths before 1906 civil registration. Indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- No statewide Pennsylvania census supplements the federal gaps.
- **The 1900 census is especially important for Irish immigrants:** it records how many years the person has been in the United States and whether they are naturalized, first papers declared, or alien.

### Probate Records

FamilySearch collection **"Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994"** (collection ID `1999196`): 2,304,118 images. This is a massive collection.

FamilySearch also has a dedicated **Schuylkill County Probate Records** volume (image group `007936749`), covering 1851–1930, 412 images: **browse-only, 0% indexed, not full-text.** A broader Pennsylvania-state-level probate volume (image group `008120441`, 1,180 images, 1683–1994) is similarly **browse-only.**

Wills and estate inventories can document family relationships, real property (company housing was common in patch towns and may not appear), and personal property. Miners rarely owned real estate but sometimes left personal property inventories.

### 🌟 Naturalization Records *(Critical for Irish immigrants)*

Pre-1906, any Pennsylvania court of record could naturalize — Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts all had jurisdiction ([Pennsylvania Naturalization Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records)). Declarations of intent and petitions for naturalization **name the applicant's country of origin** — the primary way to confirm Irish ancestry from a Pennsylvania court record.

- **FamilySearch Schuylkill County Naturalization Records** (image group `007936750`): 1849–1915, 298 images — **browse-only, 0% indexed.** Must be browsed image-by-image.
- **FamilySearch Pennsylvania-state Naturalization Records** (image group `008120443`): 1790–1915, 351 images — **15% name-indexed;** remainder browse-only.
- **After September 27, 1906:** Naturalization centralized in federal courts. Eastern Pennsylvania records are at **NARA Philadelphia** (900 Market Street, Philadelphia, PA). These later records are also indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Land and Deed Records

- **FamilySearch Schuylkill County Deed Records** (image group `007936752`): 1815–1900, 543 images — **22% name-indexed** (partially searchable by name); remainder browse-only.
- County recorders of deeds hold the original deed books for all six counties.
- Note: Irish miners in patch towns often lived in company-owned housing and did not hold deeds. Land records are more useful for miners who owned their homes or small farms in surrounding townships.

### ⚒️ Coal-Region Specialized Records *(Unique to this research problem)*

These sources exist outside the standard civil-record framework and are documented on the FamilySearch Wiki page [**Pennsylvania Coal Region Records**](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records):

**1. Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898**
Names approximately **41,000 colliery workers** across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Each entry includes:
- Worker's name and occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver, etc.)
- Wage rate
- **Parish of origin, where stated** — a direct link to Irish church records

This index covers Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland area collieries. It is the most direct finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were recorded inconsistently in census records.

**2. Company Payroll Ledgers (Schuylkill County)**
Mining company employment records and payroll ledgers listing worker names, nationalities, and sometimes prior residence are held at the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County**, Pottsville ([Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Coal_Mining_Records)). These are physical records — in-person visit or correspondence required.

**3. Mine Inspector Reports**
The Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines issued annual mine inspection reports organized by colliery. These are **not personal name indexes** — they are accident reports and safety inspections organized by colliery name — but accident reports can name miners who were killed or injured. These are at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** and partially digitized.

**4. Molly Maguires Records (Schuylkill County, 1875–1877)**
Trial transcripts, depositions, and Pinkerton detective reports from the Molly Maguires prosecutions **name hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families** across Schuylkill County and neighboring counties ([Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires)). Court records from Schuylkill County Court of Quarter Sessions. These are an adversarial but genealogically rich source for identifying Irish mining families in the 1860s–1870s.

### Tax Records

Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents **triennially from 1853** ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)). Assessment ledgers list:
- Householder name
- Real estate value
- Occupation
- Sometimes nativity

These triennial assessments serve as **census substitutes** for the missing 1890 population schedules and for years between federal enumerations. They are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at county historical societies; digitization status varies by county.

Ancestry also holds **Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801** (pre-period background), though these predate our target window.

### Military Records

- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Pennsylvania contributed heavily to the Union Army. Irish miners served in regiments including the 48th Pennsylvania Infantry. Service records and pension files are at **NARA** and indexed on Fold3/Ancestry. Pension files often contain detailed biographical information including place of birth in Ireland, wife's name, and children's names.
- **Civil War Draft Registration (1863):** The Consolidated Lists of Civil War Draft Registrations name all men 20–45 in 1863, including immigrants. These cover the coal counties and are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Pennsylvania Emergency Militia musters (1862, 1863)** — state-level records at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Cemetery Records

Catholic cemeteries associated with coal-region parishes hold most Irish miner burials. Many have been indexed on:
- **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) — free; searchable by name; coverage varies by cemetery
- **BillionGraves** — some overlap with FindAGrave

Physical sexton records are held by individual parishes or cemeteries. The Miners' cemeteries in patch towns are sometimes separate from parish cemeteries — check local historical societies for records of company-maintained burial grounds.

### Newspaper Records

The coal region had an active local press that published obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, and labor news:

| Newspaper | Location | Coverage |
|-----------|----------|----------|
| **Miners' Journal** | Pottsville (Schuylkill Co.) | 1825–present |
| **Scranton Republican** | Scranton (Lackawanna/Luzerne) | 1867–onward |
| **Wilkes-Barre Record** | Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne Co.) | 1868–onward |
| **Carbon County Gazette** | Jim Thorpe | 1850s–onward |

The **Miners' Journal** is especially important — it covered labor disputes, mining accidents (with victim names), and community events for the entire region. Digitized runs are available through **Newspapers.com** (subscription) and the **Pennsylvania State Library** microfilm collection.

### Immigration and Passenger Records

Irish coal miners arrived mainly through Philadelphia, New York, and Baltimore from the 1840s onward. Passenger lists name all persons aboard including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members.

- **FamilySearch** and **Ancestry** index federal passenger lists from major U.S. ports; indexed by name.
- **Ancestry** holds the main indexed collections: New York, Philadelphia, and Baltimore passenger arrivals.
- For immigrants before 1891, information on pre-immigration origin is sparse; naturalization declarations (above) are often a better source for county/parish of origin.

## Records NOT Online

The following record classes exist for this region but are **not available in any online database** as of the survey date:

- **Colliery payroll ledgers** (Historical Society of Schuylkill County) — physical only
- **Catholic sacramental registers** for most individual parishes — held by parish, Diocese of Scranton, or Diocese of Harrisburg; not digitized as a class
- **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments** — partially at PA State Archives; not comprehensively digitized
- **Mine inspector accident reports** — PA State Archives; partial digitization only
- **Molly Maguires trial transcripts and Pinkerton reports** — Schuylkill County court records; physical only
- **Schuylkill County Naturalization Records 1849–1915** — digitized but **browse-only** (not name-indexed)
- **Schuylkill County Marriage Records 1870–1910** — digitized but **browse-only**

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1890 Federal Census:** The population schedules are almost entirely destroyed for all Pennsylvania counties. Veterans' schedules (1890 Special Census of Union Veterans) survive and are indexed.
- **Incomplete vital registration 1852–1905:** Pennsylvania's attempts at county-level birth and death registration before 1906 produced highly incomplete returns. Absence in a pre-1906 civil registration record is not evidence of absence of the person.
- No major courthouse fires are documented for the six coal counties during the target period, but individual parish record losses (fire, flood, institutional closure) vary — always check with the diocese for known gaps.

## 🌟 FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Coal Region Records

*(Requested read — full content of this specialized page)*

The FamilySearch Wiki page [**Pennsylvania Coal Region Records**](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) documents three specialized indexes unique to the anthracite counties:

> **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898** — Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated.

> **Parish Survival** — Many Catholic parishes in the coal region were established between 1840 and 1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities. Baptismal registers for these parishes are held by the Diocese of Scranton (post-1868) and the Diocese of Harrisburg (pre-1868).

> **Tax Records** — Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853; the assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity.

The page also distinguishes **company payroll indexes** (name individual workers — the best genealogical finding aid) from **mine-inspection and accident reports** (organized by colliery, not by person — secondary genealogical use).

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with census, then push into church records.** The 1880 (full household relationships) and 1900 (years in US, naturalization status) censuses anchor the family. Use them to identify the parish district, then pivot to Catholic baptismal and marriage registers held by the Diocese of Scranton or Harrisburg. ([Pennsylvania Genealogy – Census Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records))

2. **The Lackawanna County split is a hard research wall.** If your family was in Scranton, Carbondale, or Dunmore before 1878, all their records — deeds, court, naturalization, church diocesan records — were filed in **Luzerne County.** Always search Luzerne first for pre-1878 events, then both counties for 1878–1900. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

3. **Use the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index as a first-pass locator.** Its ~41,000 entries, including parish of origin for many workers, can place your Irish ancestor at a specific colliery and provide a parish pointer before you search diocesan registers. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

4. **Naturalization pre-1906 = any county court.** Declarations of intent can appear in Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, or Orphans' Court for any of the six counties. Search all courts in the county where your ancestor lived. The FamilySearch Schuylkill naturalization volume (1849–1915) is **browse-only** — plan time to browse by approximate date. ([Pennsylvania Naturalization Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records))

5. **The 1890 census gap is bridged by triennial tax assessments.** Pennsylvania assessed coal-region residents every three years from 1853, listing occupation and sometimes nativity. These records at the PA State Archives fill the gap left by the destroyed 1890 census. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

6. **For Molly Maguires families in Schuylkill County (1860s–1870s):** Trial transcripts and Pinkerton detective reports name hundreds of Irish miners by name, townland, and family connection. Even if your ancestor was not a defendant, these records may name witnesses, neighbors, and relatives. ([Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy – Molly Maguires](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires))

7. **Church records switch dioceses at 1868.** For Catholic parish records anywhere in the six coal counties, events before 1868 fall under the **Archdiocese of Philadelphia**; after 1868, under **Diocese of Scranton** (northern counties) or **Diocese of Harrisburg** (Schuylkill). Contact the wrong diocese and they may have no record of your parish.

8. **Browse-only volumes require an image-number finding aid.** Four of the five Schuylkill County FamilySearch volumes are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Before browsing, look for a table of contents or finding aid within the first few images of each volume — many county record volumes include an index at the front.

9. **Coal-region census spelling variance is severe.** Irish surnames were anglicized, phonetically respelled, or truncated by census enumerators unfamiliar with Irish names. Search variant spellings (O'Brien/Obrien/O Brien; Gallagher/Gallacher/Gallaghar) and use Soundex options where available.

10. **Miners' Journal (Pottsville) is a primary source.** It covered the entire coal region and published mining accident victim lists, strike notices naming workers, court proceedings, and obituaries for six decades. Search digitized runs on Newspapers.com and request microfilm through the Pennsylvania State Library.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood Period, ca. 1750–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Status during target period:** Vermont was not an organized U.S. state or territory. The territory moved through three overlapping jurisdictional phases:
  - **New Hampshire Grants era (ca. 1749–1764):** NH Governor Benning Wentworth issued over 100 township grants west of the Connecticut River. The British Crown ruled in 1764 that the boundary between NH and NY ran along the Connecticut River's west bank, placing Vermont under New York's claim.
  - **New York claim era (1764–1777):** New York asserted sovereignty and issued competing patents, refusing to honor NH grants. NH grantees — led by Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys — resisted by force.
  - **Vermont Republic (1777–1791):** Vermont declared independence in January 1777, adopted its own constitution (the first in the Americas to ban adult male slavery), and organized counties and towns under Republic authority. Vermont was admitted as the 14th state on **March 4, 1791**.
- **FamilySearch standardPlace:** "Vermont, United States" (date range: +1791/). FamilySearch does not maintain a separate pre-statehood jurisdiction entry; all research tooling points to the post-1791 state.
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by tools. Vermont was sparsely settled before the Revolution; the 1791 federal census counted approximately 85,000 residents.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, timber, potash and pearl ash production, small-scale trade along the Connecticut River and Lake Champlain corridor.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descent settlers migrating from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island; Scottish, Scots-Irish, and Dutch families along the western border near Lake Champlain; French Canadian settlers in the far northwest.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant, especially in eastern Vermont towns settled from CT and MA); Baptist; Methodist (arriving ca. 1780s–90s); Episcopal/Anglican; small Quaker communities; Catholic (primarily French Canadian settlers, northwest).
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763, which depopulated the region and delayed settlement); NH Grants controversy; Revolutionary War (1775–1783), including the Battle of Bennington (1777) and Saratoga campaign; Vermont Republic period (1777–1791).

---

## Boundary changes

During this period the boundaries of the Vermont territory were actively contested:

- **Pre-1764:** Claimed by New Hampshire as part of its western extent; NH grants issued beginning ca. 1749.
- **1764:** Crown ruling transferred jurisdiction to New York; NY refused to honor NH grants.
- **1777–1791:** Vermont Republic established its own county structure independent of both NH and NY. Counties organized during the Republic period (relevant to the pre-statehood window):

| County | Organized |
|---|---|
| Bennington | 1778 |
| Windham | 1781 |
| Windsor | 1781 |
| Rutland | 1781 |
| Orange | 1781 |
| Addison | 1785 |
| Chittenden | 1787 |

Records created before 1777 in the NH-grant townships were kept at the town level by proprietors and early settlers. NY-era patents are held in New York State archives. Vermont Republic records (county courts, probate, town records) are held at Vermont state and county repositories.

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** Records for the same land and the same grantee family may exist under **three separate systems** — a NH grant, a competing NY patent, and a Vermont Republic confirmation. All three must be checked.

---

## Available record types

### ★ The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (most important pre-statehood record)

The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) specifically highlights this record:

> "The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood, enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists **grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status**. This record predates any Vermont civil registration and is the **earliest systematic resident list for the future state**."

If an ancestor held a New Hampshire grant in the Vermont territory, this document is the first place to look. It predates any civil registration and any county record structure.

---

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Statewide registration start:** Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)), statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in **1857** — nearly 70 years after statehood and entirely outside the pre-statehood window.
- **Town clerk records:** The same wiki page notes "earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive **unevenly**." Individual Vermont towns began recording vital events at settlement; some towns have records from the 1760s–1780s, but coverage varies widely by town.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices hold originals. Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) holds microfilmed copies for many towns. The FamilySearch Catalog lists digitized town vital records under individual Vermont town names.
- **Access level:** Uneven — some towns are **indexed + images** on FamilySearch; many are **microfilm-only** or **physical only** at the town office. The wiki advises consulting town clerk offices directly.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; family Bible records; probate files (which name heirs and ages); gravestone inscriptions; published town histories.

---

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (most common); Baptist; Methodist (arriving ca. 1780s–90s); Episcopal; Quaker meetings in some towns.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists, church minutes, disciplinary records.
- **Where held:** Original records at local churches or denominational archives; Vermont Historical Society (Montpelier) and Vermont State Archives hold some collections. FamilySearch has microfilmed some Vermont church records — check the FamilySearch Catalog by town.
- **Coverage note:** Many Vermont frontier settlements in the 1760s–1780s lacked organized congregations for years after founding. Church records from the very early settlement period are sparse; a missing church record in this era is common and should not be treated as evidence of a missing event.

---

### Town proprietors' records

Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)), 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." Proprietors' records document the original grantees who organized each township's land distribution.

- **Where held:** Individual town offices (originals); Vermont State Archives; Vermont Historical Society. Reprinted in published town histories widely available in library collections, Google Books, and Archive.org.
- **Access level:** Mostly **physical only** for originals; published reprints are broadly accessible.

---

### Census records

- **1790 Federal Census:** Vermont was included in the first federal census (enumerated 1790). This is the earliest systematic population count and falls at the very end of the pre-statehood period. Available **indexed + images** free on FamilySearch and by subscription on Ancestry.com.
- **Pre-1790 enumerations:** No formal federal census preceded 1790. Tax lists, militia muster rolls, and proprietors' records serve as population surrogates.
- **Access:** Ancestry.com lists the U.S. Federal Census Collection ([Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) as a curated external resource for this period.

---

### Probate and court records

- **Vermont Republic probate:** The Vermont Republic established county probate courts ca. 1778–1782. Probate records from the pre-statehood period survive at county probate court offices and have been partially microfilmed.
- **Record types:** Wills, inventories, letters of administration, guardianship records, dower rights.
- **Where held:** Vermont county probate court offices hold originals. Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) holds many microfilmed copies. Check the FamilySearch Catalog under individual Vermont county names.
- **Pre-Republic probate (deaths before 1777):** For deaths before 1777, New Hampshire or New York probate jurisdictions may hold relevant records — NH Probate Courts (NH State Archives) or NY Surrogate's Court records (New York State Archives, Albany).
- **Access level:** Partially **microfilm**; partially **physical only** at county offices.

---

### Land records

Three competing land grant systems all created records for the same Vermont territory and must all be searched:

| System | Date range | Where held |
|---|---|---|
| **New Hampshire grants** (Wentworth grants) | ca. 1749–1764 | NH State Archives (Concord, NH); published in *State Papers of New Hampshire* |
| **New York patents** | 1764–1777 | New York State Archives (Albany, NY) |
| **Vermont Republic grants & confirmations** | 1777–1791 | Vermont State Archives; VT Secretary of State |

- **Town-level land records:** After a township was organized, the town clerk recorded deeds, mortgages, and land transfers. Held at town offices, partially microfilmed by FamilySearch (check Catalog by town name).
- **Access level:** NH and NY records are largely **physical only**; published NH State Papers volumes are widely available in libraries. Vermont town deeds: varies by town — some **microfilm**, some **physical only**.

---

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783). Vermont men served in the Continental Army, state militia, and the Green Mountain Boys. Key engagements include Ticonderoga (1775), Hubbardton (1777), Bennington (1777), and Saratoga (1777).
- **Record types:**
  - Federal pension files (NARA)
  - Continental Army service records (NARA)
  - Vermont state militia records (Vermont State Archives)
  - Bounty land warrant records (NARA)
- **Online access:**
  - **Fold3** ([Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) — Revolutionary War service records and pension files (subscription) — returned as a curated FS external resource for this period
  - **Ancestry.com** ([Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) — NARA-sourced pension and service records (subscription)
  - **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) — holds originals; many digitized via Fold3/Ancestry
- **Vermont-specific:** Vermont adjutant general's records of Revolutionary War service are held at Vermont State Archives. The DAR Patriot Index is a finding aid for confirmed patriots with documented service.

---

### Tax records

- **Vermont Republic taxes:** The Vermont Republic levied taxes on real and personal property from the late 1770s onward. Tax lists survive for some towns and counties.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives; Vermont Historical Society. Some published by the Vermont Historical Society and local genealogical societies.
- **Substitute value:** The best available census substitute for the pre-1790 period — tax lists appear annually and name heads of household with taxable property.
- **Access level:** Largely **physical only** (Vermont State Archives / Vermont Historical Society).

---

### Cemetery records

- **Frontier-era burials:** Town (municipal) cemeteries and church graveyards are primary burial sites. Earliest burials (1760s–1780s) may be in farmstead family plots or small community cemeteries, some now lost.
- **Online coverage:**
  - **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) — widespread Vermont coverage, free — returned as a curated FS external resource for this period.
  - BillionGraves covers some Vermont cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are at town offices or local historical societies. DAR gravestone inscription projects of the early 20th century produced transcriptions held at Vermont Historical Society and the DAR library (Washington, DC).

---

### Newspapers

- **First Vermont newspapers:** Vermont's earliest papers began in the late 1770s–1780s (e.g., *Vermont Gazette*, Bennington, ca. 1781; *Vermont Journal*, Windsor, ca. 1783). Coverage for the pre-statehood period is thin but growing.
- **Content value:** Marriage and death notices, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), political news of the Republic period.
- **Where held:**
  - **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) — some early Vermont newspapers (subscription) — returned as a curated FS external resource.
  - Vermont State Library; Vermont Historical Society; University of Vermont Bailey/Howe Library.
  - Vermont Digital Newspaper Project (free, hosted by University of Vermont) — digitized early issues.

---

### Immigration / emigration records

- **Context:** The Vermont territory in the late 1700s was primarily a destination for internal migrants from southern New England, not an international port of entry. International immigration was minimal in this period.
- **French Canadian settlers:** The northwest (Champlain Valley) had French Canadian families; search Quebec parish registers alongside Vermont records.
- **Origin-community searches:** If ancestors migrated to Vermont from another colony/state, search records in their origin communities (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, New York, New Hampshire) for earlier generations and collateral family.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Coverage for this period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | 1790 census (indexed + images); some town vital records; some probate/land records (check FamilySearch Catalog by town/county name) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 census (indexed + images); Revolutionary War pension files; some VT town records | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Revolutionary War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Some early Vermont newspapers | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Vermont cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| Vermont Digital Newspaper Project | Digitized early Vermont newspaper issues | Free |
| Google Books / Archive.org | Published Vermont town histories (1860–1900) reprinting colonial-era proprietors' records | Free |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives & Records Administration (Montpelier, VT) | Town vital records (microfilm); probate records; land records; tax lists; Vermont Republic records; militia records | In-person; some microfilm loan |
| Vermont Historical Society (Montpelier, VT) | Town histories; DAR gravestone transcriptions; family papers; church records; newspapers | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Vermont county probate court offices | Original probate files from Republic period onward (1778–) | In-person / mail |
| Vermont town clerk offices | Original town vital records, land records, proprietors' records (varies by town) | In-person / mail |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | NH Governor Wentworth grant records; NH probate (for pre-1777 deaths) | In-person / mail |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | NY patent records; NY colonial court records for VT territory | In-person; online finding aids |
| NARA (Washington, DC / College Park, MD) | 1790 census; Revolutionary War service and pension records; bounty land warrants | In-person; many records on Fold3/Ancestry |

---

## Records NOT online

- Vermont town clerk vital records prior to 1857 are highly uneven online. Many are **microfilm-only or physical-only**; the FamilySearch Catalog (searched by specific town name) will reveal what has been digitized for each town.
- Vermont Republic tax lists are largely **physical-only** (Vermont State Archives / Vermont Historical Society).
- New Hampshire Wentworth-era township grant records are **physical** at the NH State Archives; published volumes of the *State Papers of New Hampshire* (available at many research libraries) are the most accessible pathway.
- New York colonial patent records for the Vermont territory are **physical** at the New York State Archives.
- Vermont Republic county court records (civil suits, criminal cases) from 1777–1791 are largely **physical-only** at county courthouses.
- Early Vermont church records (most denominations) remain at local parish offices with no digital access.

> ⚠️ **Survey gap:** The FamilySearch `collections_search` and `volume_search` tools were not available in this research environment. The guide above cannot report specific FamilySearch collection IDs, record counts, or digitization percentages. Search the FamilySearch Catalog directly at **familysearch.org/catalog**, filtered to "Vermont" or to individual town/county names, to identify all microfilmed and digitized holdings not captured here.

---

## Known record losses

The FamilySearch Vermont wiki results returned no specific record destruction events (courthouse fires, floods, wartime losses) for this period. The primary research challenge for pre-statehood Vermont is **incompleteness of record creation** rather than destruction: frontier settlement conditions of the 1760s–1780s meant that organized civil record-keeping was slow to develop, congregations often lacked permanent clergy for years after founding, and many early events were never formally recorded. Absence of a record should be treated as a known gap to work around, not as evidence that the event didn't occur.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.** Per the FamilySearch wiki ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)), this is the earliest systematic resident list for Vermont, predating any civil registration. ~1,800 NH grantees are named with township, acreage, and disputed-claim status.

2. **No statewide vital registration before 1857.** The FamilySearch wiki ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) is unambiguous: statewide registration began 1857. Town clerk records go back to the 1770s in some towns but are uneven — search the FamilySearch Catalog under the specific town name, then contact the town clerk directly.

3. **Town histories are primary-source repositories.** The FamilySearch wiki ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) calls out 19th-century town histories (1860–1900) as reprinting colonial-era proprietors' records "otherwise difficult to access." Start with the published history for any Vermont town in your research. Many are free on Google Books and Archive.org.

4. **Check all three land-grant systems.** For any pre-1791 land transaction or family settlement, search NH grant records, NY patent records, AND Vermont Republic confirmation records. The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is the key finding aid.

5. **The 1790 federal census is your earliest population count.** Vermont was included and the census is available free on FamilySearch. Use it as an anchor point and work backward using tax lists and proprietors' records.

6. **Tax lists are the best pre-1790 census substitute.** Vermont Republic tax lists (late 1770s–1780s) name heads of household annually. They are largely physical-only at the Vermont State Archives and Vermont Historical Society.

7. **Search adjoining jurisdictions across state lines.** Western Vermont families (Chittenden, Addison counties) may have records in upstate New York (Clinton, Franklin, Washington counties, NY). Eastern Vermont families along the Connecticut River should be cross-checked against New Hampshire towns directly across the river (Grafton, Sullivan, Cheshire counties, NH). French Canadian families in the northwest may have records in Quebec parish registers.

8. **Revolutionary War records are rich.** Vermont men appear in federal NARA pension files (on Fold3 and Ancestry) and Vermont state militia records (Vermont State Archives). 9. **Curated FamilySearch external links for Vermont (1750–1800) were generic.** The six resources returned (Ancestry census, FamilySearch vital records wiki, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) are not Vermont-specific. Consult the FamilySearch Vermont wiki page ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) directly for updated repository and collection links.

- The **1771 Grant Survey Schedule** is the single most important pre-statehood record: ~1,800 NH grantees listed with township, acreage, and disputed-claim status — "the earliest systematic resident list for the future state."
- **Statewide civil registration began in 1857** — far outside your window. Before that, town clerk records go back to the 1770s in some towns but survive unevenly; the wiki explicitly directs researchers to contact town clerks directly.
- **19th-century town histories** (1860–1900) routinely reprint colonial-era proprietors' records "otherwise difficult to access" — these are primary sources hiding inside published volumes.

The `getting_started`, `online_records`, and `research_tips` wiki sections returned no separate content for Vermont; only the home section exists in the current FS wiki corpus. The `collections_search` and `volume_search` tools were not available in this environment, so specific FS collection IDs and digitization percentages could not be reported — use the FamilySearch Catalog directly at **familysearch.org/catalog** filtered to Vermont or a specific town/county.

1. **Triple land-grant system.** Every piece of Vermont land may have a New Hampshire Wentworth grant, a competing New York patent, *and* a Vermont Republic confirmation. You must check all three — NH State Archives, NY State Archives, and Vermont State Archives — for the same family.
